text:
Dask Use Cases



Use cases


Dask is used in multiple fields such as:

Geospatial
Finance
Astrophysics
Microbiology
Environmental science

Check out the Dask use cases page that provides a number of sample workflows.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
Dask DataFrame - parallelized pandas



Description


Looks and feels like the pandas API, but for parallel and distributed workflows.

At its core, the dask.dataframe module implements a “blocked parallel” DataFrame object that looks and feels like the pandas API, but for parallel and distributed workflows.
One Dask DataFrame is comprised of many in-memory pandas DataFrames separated along the index.
One operation on a Dask DataFrame triggers many pandas operations on the constituent pandas DataFrames in a way that is mindful of potential parallelism and memory constraints.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text: Dask DataFrame

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
Dask DataFrame



Related Documentation



DataFrame documentation
DataFrame screencast
DataFrame API
DataFrame examples
pandas documentation

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



When to use dask.dataframe


pandas is great for tabular datasets that fit in memory. A general rule of thumb for pandas is:

“Have 5 to 10 times as much RAM as the size of your dataset”


~ Wes McKinney (2017) in 10 things I hate about pandas

Here “size of dataset” means dataset size on the disk.
Dask becomes useful when the datasets exceed the above rule.
In this notebook, you will be working with the New York City Airline data. This dataset is only ~200MB, so that you can download it in a reasonable time, but dask.dataframe will scale to datasets much larger than memory.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Create datasets


Create the datasets you will be using in this notebook:
%run prep.py -d flights






Set up your local cluster


Create a local Dask cluster and connect it to the client.
from dask.distributed import Client

client = Client(n_workers=4)
client

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Dask Diagnostic Dashboard


Dask Distributed provides a useful Dashboard to visualize the state of your cluster and computations.
Click on the dashboard link displayed in the Client details above: http://127.0.0.1:8787/status. It will open a new browser tab with the Dashboard.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Reading and working with datasets


Let’s read an extract of flights in the USA across several years. This data is specific to flights out of the three airports in the New York City area.
import os
import dask
By convention, we import the module dask.dataframe as dd, and call the corresponding DataFrame object ddf.









Note


The term “Dask DataFrame” is slightly overloaded. Depending on the context, it can refer to the module or the DataFrame object. To avoid confusion:

dask.dataframe (note the all lowercase) refers to the API, and
DataFrame (note the CamelCase) refers to the object.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Reading and working with datasets


The following filename includes a glob pattern *, so all files in the path matching that pattern will be read into the same DataFrame.
import dask.dataframe as dd

ddf = dd.read_csv(
    os.path.join("data", "nycflights", "*.csv"), parse_dates={"Date": [0, 1, 2]}
)
ddf

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



What happened?


Dask has not loaded the data yet, it has:

investigated the input path and found that there are ten matching files
intelligently created a set of jobs for each chunk – one per original CSV file in this case










Note


Notice that the representation of the DataFrame object contains no data - Dask has just done enough to read the start of the first file, and infer the column names and dtypes.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Lazy Evaluation


Most Dask Collections, including Dask DataFrame are evaluated lazily, which means Dask constructs the logic (called task graph) of your computation immediately but “evaluates” them only when necessary.
You can view this task graph using .visualize().
ddf.visualize()
Note that we need to call .compute() to trigger actual computations.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Lazy Evaluation


Some functions like len and head also trigger a computation. Specifically, calling len will:

load actual data, (that is, load each file into a pandas DataFrame)
then apply the corresponding functions to each pandas DataFrame (also known as a partition)
combine the subtotals to give you the final grand total

# load and count number of rows
len(ddf)

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Lazy Evaluation


You can view the start and end of the data as you would in pandas:
ddf.head()
ddf.tail()

# ValueError: Mismatched dtypes found in `pd.read_csv`/`pd.read_table`.

# +----------------+---------+----------+
# | Column         | Found   | Expected |
# +----------------+---------+----------+
# | CRSElapsedTime | float64 | int64    |
# | TailNum        | object  | float64  |
# +----------------+---------+----------+

# The following columns also raised exceptions on conversion:

# - TailNum
#   ValueError("could not convert string to float: 'N54711'")

# Usually this is due to dask's dtype inference failing, and
# *may* be fixed by specifying dtypes manually by adding:

# dtype={'CRSElapsedTime': 'float64',
#        'TailNum': 'object'}

# to the call to `read_csv`/`read_table`.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Handling conflicting types


Unlike pandas.read_csv which reads in the entire file before inferring datatypes, dask.dataframe.read_csv only reads in a sample from the beginning of the file (or first file if using a glob). These inferred datatypes are then enforced when reading all partitions.
In this case, the datatypes inferred in the sample are incorrect. The first n rows have no value for CRSElapsedTime (which pandas infers as a float), and later on turn out to be strings (object dtype). When this happens you have a few options:

Specify dtypes directly using the dtype keyword. This is the recommended solution, as it’s the least error prone (better to be explicit than implicit) and also the most performant.
Increase the size of the sample keyword (in bytes)
Use assume_missing to make dask assume that columns inferred to be int (which don’t allow missing values) are actually floats (which do allow missing values). In our particular case this doesn’t apply.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Handling conflicting types


In our case we’ll use the first option and directly specify the dtypes of the offending columns.
ddf = dd.read_csv(
    os.path.join("data", "nycflights", "*.csv"),
    parse_dates={"Date": [0, 1, 2]},
    dtype={"TailNum": str, "CRSElapsedTime": float, "Cancelled": bool},
)
ddf.tail()  # now works

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Reading from remote storage


If you’re thinking about distributed computing, your data is probably stored remotely on services (like Amazon’s S3 or Google’s cloud storage) and is in a friendlier format (like Parquet). Dask can read data in various formats directly from these remote locations lazily and in parallel.
Here’s how you can read the NYC taxi cab data from Amazon S3:
ddf = dd.read_parquet(
    "s3://nyc-tlc/trip data/yellow_tripdata_2012-*.parquet",
)
You can also leverage Parquet-specific optimizations like column selection and metadata handling, learn more in the Dask documentation on working with Parquet files.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Computations with dask.dataframe


Let’s compute the maximum of the flight delay.
With just pandas, we would loop over each file to find the individual maximums, then find the final maximum over all the individual maximums.
import pandas as pd

files = os.listdir(os.path.join('data', 'nycflights'))

maxes = []

for file in files:
    df = pd.read_csv(os.path.join('data', 'nycflights', file))
    maxes.append(df.DepDelay.max())
    
final_max = max(maxes)

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Computations with dask.dataframe


dask.dataframe lets us write pandas-like code, that operates on larger-than-memory datasets in parallel.
%%time
result = ddf.DepDelay.max()
result.compute()
This creates the lazy computation for us and then runs it.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame






Computations with dask.dataframe


Dask will delete intermediate results (like the full pandas DataFrame for each file) as soon as possible. This means you can handle datasets that are larger than memory but, repeated computations will have to load all of the data in each time. (Run the code above again, is it faster or slower than you would expect?)
You can view the underlying task graph using .visualize():
# notice the parallelism
result.visualize()

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Sharing Intermediate Results


When computing all of the above, we sometimes did the same operation more than once. For most operations, dask.dataframe stores the arguments, allowing duplicate computations to be shared and only computed once.
For example, let’s compute the mean and standard deviation for departure delay of all non-canceled flights.
If you compute them with two calls to compute, there is no sharing of intermediate computations.
non_canceled = ddf[~ddf.Cancelled]
mean_delay = non_canceled.DepDelay.mean()
std_delay = non_canceled.DepDelay.std()
#| tags: []
%%time

mean_delay_res = mean_delay.compute()
std_delay_res = std_delay.compute()

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



dask.compute


But let’s try by passing both to a single compute call.
#| tags: []
%%time

mean_delay_res, std_delay_res = dask.compute(mean_delay, std_delay)
Using dask.compute takes roughly 1/2 the time. This is because the task graphs for both results are merged when calling dask.compute, allowing shared operations to only be done once instead of twice. In particular, using dask.compute only does the following once:

the calls to read_csv
the filter (df[~df.Cancelled])
some of the necessary reductions (sum, count)

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



Visualization



To see what the merged task graphs between multiple results look like (and what’s shared), you can use the dask.visualize function
you might want to use filename='graph.pdf' to save the graph to disk so that you can zoom in more easily

dask.visualize(mean_delay, std_delay, engine="cytoscape")

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



.persist()


While using a distributed scheduler (you will learn more about schedulers in the upcoming notebooks), you can keep some data that you want to use often in the distributed memory.
persist generates “Futures” (more on this later as well) and stores them in the same structure as your output. You can use persist with any data or computation that fits in memory.
If you want to analyze data only for non-canceled flights departing from JFK airport, you can either have two compute calls like in the previous section:
non_cancelled = ddf[~ddf.Cancelled]
ddf_jfk = non_cancelled[non_cancelled.Origin == "JFK"]
%%time
ddf_jfk.DepDelay.mean().compute()
ddf_jfk.DepDelay.sum().compute()

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
DataFrame



.persist()


Or, consider persisting that subset of data in memory.
See the “Graph” dashboard plot, the red squares indicate persisted data stored as Futures in memory. You will also notice an increase in Worker Memory (another dashboard plot) consumption.
ddf_jfk = ddf_jfk.persist()  # returns back control immediately
%%time

What is meta?


Since Dask operates lazily, it doesn’t always have enough information to infer the output structure (which includes datatypes) of certain operations.
meta is a suggestion to Dask about the output of your computation. Importantly, meta never infers with the output structure. Dask uses this meta until it can determine the actual output structure.
Even though there are many ways to define meta, we suggest using a small pandas Series or DataFrame that matches the structure of your final output.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
Dask Arrays



Too small is a problem



If your chunks are too small, the amount of actual work done by every task is very tiny, and the overhead of coordinating all these tasks results in a very inefficient process.
In general, the dask scheduler takes approximately one millisecond to coordinate a single task. That means we want the computation time to be comparatively large, i.e in the order of seconds.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
Dask Arrays



Too big is a problem



If your chunks are too big, this is also a problem because you will likely run out of memory.
You will start seeing in the dashboard that data is being spill to disk and this will lead to performance decrements.
If we load to much data into memory, Dask workers will start to spill data to disk to avoid crashing.
To watch out for this you can look at the worker memory plot on the dashboard.
Orange bars are a warning you are close to the limit, and gray means data is being spilled to disk.

title: Big Data: Dask tutorial
text:
Dask Arrays



Rules of thumb



Users have reported that chunk sizes smaller than 1MB tend to be bad. In general, a chunk size between 100MB and 1GB is good, while going over 1 or 2GB means you have a really big dataset and/or a lot of memory available per worker.
Upper bound: Avoid very large task graphs. More than 10,000 or 100,000 chunks may start to perform poorly.
Lower bound: To get the advantage of parallelization, you need the number of chunks to at least equal the number of worker cores available (or better, the number of worker cores times 2). Otherwise, some workers will stay idle.
The time taken to compute each task should be much larger than the time needed to schedule the task. The Dask scheduler takes roughly 1 millisecond to coordinate a single task, so a good task computation time would be in the order of seconds (not milliseconds).
Chunks should be aligned with array storage on disk. Modern NDArray storage formats (HDF5, NetCDF, TIFF, Zarr) allow arrays to be stored in chunks so that the blocks of data can be pulled efficiently. However, data stores often chunk more finely than is ideal for Dask array, so it is common to choose a chunking that is a multiple of your storage chunk size, otherwise you might incur high overhead. For example, if you are loading data that is chunked in blocks of (100, 100), the you might might choose a chunking strategy more like (1000, 2000) that is larger but still divisible by (100, 100).

For more more advice on chunking see https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/array-chunks.html

text:
Moore’s Law



Definition (1965)


Number of transistors in an integrated circuit (IC) doubles about every two years.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text: Moore’s Law

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text: Moore’s Law

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Moore’s Law



Trends



Gordon Moore: Moore’s law will end by around 2025.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: declared Moore’s law dead in 2022.







Pat Gelsinger, Intel CEO, end of 2023



We’re no longer in the golden era of Moore’s Law, it’s much, much harder now, so we’re probably doubling effectively closer to every three years now, so we’ve definitely seen a slowing.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Edholm’s law



Definition (2004)



three categories of telecommunication, namely

wireless (mobile),
nomadic (wireless without mobility)
and wired networks (fixed),

are in lockstep and gradually converging
the bandwidth and data rates double every 18 months, which has proven to be true since the 1970s

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text: Edholm’s law

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Edholm’s law




Data deluge



90% of data humankind has produced happened in the last two years.
80% of data could be unstructured
99% of data produced is never analyzed

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Dennard scaling



Definition (Robert Dennard, 1974)


As transistors get smaller, their power density stays roughly constant – smaller transistors run at proportionally lower voltage and current.






Why it mattered


For ~30 years this is what let clock speeds climb alongside Moore’s Law: each new process node gave you more transistors and a higher safe clock at the same power budget. Software got faster for free.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
The power wall



Dennard scaling broke down (~2006)


Below roughly 65 nm, leakage current and heat stopped shrinking with the transistors. More switching in the same area now means more power and more heat than the chip can dissipate.






Consequence


Clock speed hit a ceiling. The Pentium 4 reached ~3.8 GHz in 2004; twenty years later, mainstream CPUs still run at ~3–5 GHz.






“The Free Lunch Is Over” – Herb Sutter, 2005


Single-thread performance now grows only a few percent per year. Making code faster became a parallelism problem, not a “wait for next year’s CPU” problem.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
The multicore pivot



Same transistors, spent differently


Moore’s Law kept delivering transistors – vendors just stopped spending them on faster cores and started spending them on more cores.

2005: first mainstream dual-core desktop chips (Athlon 64 X2, Pentium D)
today: 8–16 cores on a laptop, 64–192 in a server socket

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Beyond more cores



Data-level parallelism: SIMD


One instruction, many elements:

SSE (128-bit)
AVX2 (256)
AVX-512 (512)
ARM NEON / SVE







Domain-specific hardware:



GPUs (thousands of simple cores, huge memory bandwidth)
TPUs (matrix-multiply units)
FPGAs.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
What to do now?



Choices



Use all the cores – threads / processes (next section)
Use SIMD – via vectorised libraries: NumPy, Polars, DuckDB
Use accelerators – GPUs for the right workloads
Be smart – better algorithms, cache-friendly data layout, better data formats

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text: Core counts

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Concurrency vs Parallelism





Concurrency


Individual steps of both tasks are executed in an interleaved fashion







Parallelism


Task statements are executed at the same time.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Process



Definition


A process can be defined as an instance of a running program with its own memory.
Alternatively: a context maintained for an executing program.
Processes have:

lifetimes
parents
children.
memory/resources allocated.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text: Process

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Threads



Definition


A lightweight unit of execution within a process that can operate independently.
Thread is a basic unit to which the operating system allocates processor time.
Managed with help of thread context, which consists of processor context and information required for thread management.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text: Threads

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text: Comparison table

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Green threads/Coroutines



Definition


These are threads managed by the process runtime, multiplexed onto OS threads.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
The GIL



Global Interpreter Lock


CPython uses one lock that a thread must hold to execute Python bytecode.

protects reference counts and interpreter state from data races
consequence: only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time (in the default build)







So what does threading give you?


Concurrency, not CPU parallelism, for pure Python code – unless you run a free-threaded build (below).

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
When threads still help



The GIL is released…



during blocking I/O (network, disk, database) – so I/O-bound work does scale on threads
inside C extensions that explicitly drop it: NumPy, parts of pandas, scikit-learn, zlib, Numba nogil=True







Data-science nuance


A NumPy/BLAS-heavy workload can get real speedup from threading – the heavy lifting runs with the GIL released.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
multiprocessing



Real parallelism for pure-Python CPU work


Each process gets its own interpreter and its own GIL.






…but it isn’t free



process startup cost
everything crossing the boundary is pickled – expensive for large arrays / DataFrames

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
concurrent.futures & asyncio



concurrent.futures – one API, two backends


from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor

# ThreadPoolExecutor  -> I/O-bound, or GIL-releasing native code
# ProcessPoolExecutor -> CPU-bound pure Python
with ProcessPoolExecutor() as ex:
    results = list(ex.map(work, tasks, chunksize=100))






asyncio


Single thread, cooperative multitasking. Built for thousands of concurrent I/O calls (HTTP, DB). Never for CPU-bound work.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
asyncio: the event loop



Cooperative multitasking, one thread


An event loop runs coroutines. A coroutine runs until it hits await on something not yet ready (a socket, a timer), then yields control back to the loop, which runs whatever else is ready.

no preemption – a coroutine holds the CPU until it chooses to await
no GIL contention, no per-thread stack – scales to tens of thousands of open connections
one blocking call, or one CPU-heavy stretch with no await, stalls everything

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
asyncio: in practice



The pieces


import asyncio

async def fetch(url): ...                    # a coroutine

async def main():
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:    # 3.11+
        for u in urls:
            tg.create_task(fetch(u))         # scheduled concurrently

asyncio.run(main())









Issues



“function colours” – async is contagious; you need async-native libraries (aiohttp, httpx, asyncpg). A normal blocking call freezes the loop.
push unavoidable blocking / CPU work off the loop with await asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...) or loop.run_in_executor(...).

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
asyncio vs threads



Same goal (I/O concurrency), different trade-offs






threading
asyncio




scheduling
preemptive (OS)
cooperative (await)


memory per task
~MB (stack)
~KB


scales to
thousands
tens of thousands


special libraries
not needed
yes (async drivers)


accidental blocking
slows one thread
freezes everything

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Amdahl’s law



The ceiling on speedup


\(S(n)\) is the speedup with \(n\) workers: \(S(n) = T(1)\,/\,T(n)\) – single-worker time divided by \(n\)-worker time.
Normalise \(T(1) = 1\), split into a serial part \(1-p\) and a parallel part \(p\). With \(n\) workers the parallel part takes \(p/n\) while the serial part is unchanged: \[ T(n) = (1-p) + \frac{p}{n}, \qquad S(n) = \frac{1}{(1-p) + \dfrac{p}{n}}. \]
As \(n \to \infty\), \(S \to \dfrac{1}{1-p}\): a 5% serial fraction caps you at 20x, no matter the hardware.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text: Amdahl’s law

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Gustafson’s law



A different question (Gustafson, 1988)


Amdahl: same problem, more cores – how much faster? Gustafson: more cores, same wall-clock time – how much more work?
With more cores you scale the problem up (finer mesh, more data, more iterations). The serial part stays roughly fixed, so its relative weight shrinks as the problem grows.






Scaled speedup


\[ S(n) = (1-p) + p\,n \] Linear in \(n\), slope \(p\) – no hard ceiling, because \(p\) is now the parallel fraction of the bigger workload.

text: Amdahl vs Gustafson

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Sharing data without pickling



Zero-copy between processes



multiprocessing.shared_memory.SharedMemory – back a NumPy array with a shared buffer
Arrow IPC – the on-wire format is the in-memory format, so no serialization step
memory-mapped files (np.memmap)

This is how Dask and Ray move large arrays between workers cheaply.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Removing the GIL: free threading



Free-threaded CPython (PEP 703)


A build with the GIL compiled out.

experimental in 3.13, officially supported in 3.14 (PEP 779)
still opt-in (python3.14t); the GIL build stays the default
single-threaded overhead: ~40% in 3.13 -> under ~10% in 3.14
pure-Python threads finally run in parallel







How to check if present?


sys._is_gil_enabled()

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Removing the GIL: sub-interpreters



Multiple interpreters, one process (PEP 684, PEP 734)


Each interpreter gets its own GIL, so several can run Python bytecode at once – without the cost of separate OS processes.

per-interpreter GIL: C-API since 3.12 (PEP 684)
concurrent.interpreters – a pure-Python API, new in 3.14 (PEP 734)
talk over channels / shared memoryview; no pickling on the fast path

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Typing



Static vs dynamic



static: types are known and checked before running the program
dynamic: types become known when the program is running







Strong vs weak



strong: variable types are not changed easily
weak: types can be changed by the compiler if necessary

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text: Typing

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Typing: when are types checked?



Three timings



compile time – C, Rust, Java, Haskell: type errors are rejected before the program runs
run time – Python, Ruby: an operation fails when it is actually attempted
gradual – optional annotations checked by a separate tool, not the interpreter: Python + mypy / pyright / ty, or TypeScript over JavaScript







Manifest vs inferred


Do you write the types (int x = 3) or does the compiler work them out? Full inference: Haskell, ML, mostly Rust. Partial: C++ auto, C# var, Python type checkers.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Typing: nominal vs structural



What makes two types “the same”?



nominal – the declared name must match (Java, C#, Rust): a class implements an interface only if it says so
structural – the shape must match (Go interfaces, TypeScript, Python Protocol): if it has the right methods, it fits

“Duck typing” is structural typing checked at run time.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Typing & performance



Why static types make code faster



fixed types let the compiler pick a machine representation (a 64-bit int, not a boxed PyObject) and lay data out contiguously
no runtime dispatch – a + b becomes one instruction instead of “look up __add__, check types, box the result”







Python’s hints don’t do this


def f(x: int) -> int: is erased at run time – CPython ignores it. The speed-up comes only when a tool acts on the types: Cython, mypyc, Numba.

text:
Memory management



Code


import os
import gc
import psutil

proc = psutil.Process(os.getpid())

The memory wall



Why caches exist


For decades CPU throughput grew far faster than DRAM latency. That widening gap – the memory wall – is why modern chips spend most of their transistors on cache.






Consequence


“Speeding up single-node computation” is very often really: stop waiting on memory.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Cache lines



Memory moves in blocks


The CPU never fetches a single byte – it pulls in a cache line (64 bytes) at a time.






Locality



spatial – touch an address and you’ll likely touch its neighbours: lay data out contiguously, walk it in order
temporal – touch an address and you’ll likely touch it again soon: reuse before it’s evicted

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Sequential vs strided



Same element count, very different speed


a = np.zeros((10_000, 10_000))   # C-contiguous: row-major
a.sum(axis=1)   # walks each row contiguously  -- cache-friendly
a.sum(axis=0)   # jumps 10_000 floats per step -- a new cache line every access
Summing down columns of a row-major array can be several times slower, purely from cache misses – the arithmetic is identical.

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Row-major vs column-major



It’s a layout question, everywhere



NumPy: order='C' (row-major) vs order='F' (column-major) – iterate along the contiguous axis
array-of-structs vs struct-of-arrays – SoA keeps each field contiguous
columnar formats (Parquet, Arrow – Lec 1) are SoA on disk: analytics scans touch a few columns over many rows, so column layout means fewer cache lines read

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Python object overhead



Why a plain list is the slow default



a Python int is a heap object: ~28 bytes, not 8
a list of \({10}^7\) ints is \({10}^7\) pointers, each to a boxed int scattered across the heap – terrible locality
a NumPy int64 array is 8 bytes/element in one contiguous block




sys.getsizeof(10**6)                   # ~28   (the int object alone)
sys.getsizeof([0] * 1_000_000)         # ~8 MB of pointers
np.zeros(1_000_000, np.int64).nbytes   # 8 MB, contiguous and unboxed






The general lesson


Vectorised NumPy/pandas isn’t just “C is fast” – it’s contiguous, unboxed data that the cache can stream.

Views vs copies



Allocation is not free



NumPy slicing returns a view – no copy, no allocation
.copy(), fancy / boolean indexing, astype, most reshapes that can’t alias -> a new allocation
np.shares_memory(a, b) to check
pandas’ SettingWithCopyWarning is exactly this distinction leaking through

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Rust/PyO3 example



Shannon cipher


A Shannon cipher is a pair \(\mathcal{E} = (E,D)\) of functions:

The function \(E\) (the encryption function) takes as input a key \(k\) and message \(m\) (also called plaintext) and produces as output a ciphertext $c): \[
c = E(k,m)
\]

\(c\) is the encryption of \(m\) under \(k\).

The function \(D\) (the decryption function) takes as input a key \(k\) and ciphertext \(c\), and produces a message \(m\): \[
m = D(k,c)
\]

\(m\) is the decryption of \(c\) under \(k\).

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Rust/PyO3 example



Correctness property


For all keys \(k\) and messages \(m\), we have \[
D(k, E(k,m)) = m
\]

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Rust/PyO3 example



Parameters


Now we describe the cipher.
First, we define cipher parameters:

An alphabet \(A\) with size \(L \equiv |A|\).
A matrix \(M\) with size \(N \gg L\)
\(\sigma_1, \sigma_2\) are some permutations \(N \rightarrow N\)
\(\phi\) is some bit sequence of length \(P\): \(\phi \in \{0,1\}^P\)

A triple \((\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \phi)\) will be our secret key.
We define each symbol \(z\) by a corresponding set of diagonals \(D\) in the matrix \(M\), so that \(\forall (x,y) \in D: x - y = z (\mod L)\) (see Figure 1).

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Rust/PyO3 example



Encoder flow


Suppose we receive some text \(T\) containing symbols to be encoded.
For each \(t_i \in T\), obtain its numeric representation \(z_i\). \[
z_i \in [0,L)
\] Then we map each \(z_i\) to a pair of matrix coordinates \((x_i, y_i)\) such that:

First, we pick a random \(x_i \in [0,N)\) (e.g., horizontal coordinate in a matrix)
Then, we randomly pick some \(y_i \in [0,N)\) such that: \[
x_i - y_i = z_i (\mod L)
\]

title: Big Data: Speeding up computation
Big Data: Speeding up computation
text:
Rust/PyO3 example



Decoder flow


Below are steps executing during decoding phase:

Receive encoded ciphertext \(\{(\xi_i, \eta_i)\}\).
Apply inverse permutations \(\sigma_j^{-1}, \sigma_{j+1}^{-1}\): \[
(x_i,y_i) = (\sigma_j^{-1}(\xi_i), \sigma_{j+1}^{-1}(\eta_i))
\]
Find \(z_i\): \[
z_i = x_i - y_i \; (\mod L)
\]

First, install Cython and Numba:
uv add cython
uv add numba
Then we can load Cython extension in Jupyter:

%load_ext Cython

Define a function that generates a list of first \(n\) primes:






ImportantPure Python




def primes1(nb_primes):
    p = [0] * 1000
    if nb_primes > 1000:
        nb_primes = 1000

    len_p = 0  # The current number of elements in p.
    n = 2
    while len_p < nb_primes:
        # Is n prime?
        for i in p[:len_p]:
            if n % i == 0:
                break

        # If no break occurred in the loop, we have a prime.
        else:
            p[len_p] = n
            len_p += 1
        n += 1

    # Let's copy the result into a Python list:
    result_as_list = [prime for prime in p[:len_p]]
    return result_as_list

Define functions that will be applied to the DataFrame:






ImportantPure Python




def f(x):

def integrate_f(a, b, N):
    s = 0
    dx = (b - a) / N
    for i in range(N):
        s += f(a + i * dx)

    dx: cython.double

PyO3 (Rust)
Cython is a dialect – Python plus C type declarations, compiled through C. PyO3 takes a different route: write the extension in Rust, a real systems language, and expose functions to Python. You get memory safety, cargo’s package ecosystem, and modern tooling – at the cost of learning Rust and a heavier build step. It has become the default way to write Rust extensions for Python (used by pydantic-core, polars, cryptography, ruff, …).
Prerequisites: a Rust toolchain (rustup / cargo) and the maturin build tool:
uv add --dev maturin
The crate lives in _files/integ_rs/ and has three files:
_files/integ_rs/Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "integ_rs"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[lib]
name = "integ_rs"
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
pyo3 = { version = "0.27", features = ["extension-module"] }

[profile.release]
opt-level = 3
lto = true
_files/integ_rs/pyproject.toml – tells maturin how to build:
[build-system]
requires = ["maturin>=1.7,<2.0"]
build-backend = "maturin"

[project]
name = "integ_rs"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.14"

[tool.maturin]
bindings = "pyo3"
_files/integ_rs/src/lib.rs – the same integrate_f as before, in Rust:
use pyo3::prelude::*;

#[inline]
fn f(x: f64) -> f64 {
    x * (x - 1.0)
}

/// Numeric integration of f from a to b using n rectangles.
#[pyfunction]
fn integrate_f(a: f64, b: f64, n: i64) -> f64 {
    let dx = (b - a) / n as f64;
    let mut s = 0.0;
    for i in 0..n {
        s += f(a + i as f64 * dx);
    }
    s * dx
}

/// Apply integrate_f over whole columns in one call.
#[pyfunction]
fn apply_integrate_f(a: Vec<f64>, b: Vec<f64>, n: Vec<i64>) -> Vec<f64> {
    a.iter()
        .zip(b.iter())
        .zip(n.iter())
        .map(|((&ai, &bi), &ni)| integrate_f(ai, bi, ni))
        .collect()
}

#[pymodule]
fn integ_rs(m: &Bound<'_, PyModule>) -> PyResult<()> {
    m.add_function(wrap_pyfunction!(integrate_f, m)?)?;
    m.add_function(wrap_pyfunction!(apply_integrate_f, m)?)?;
    Ok(())
}
Build it into the current environment (--release for optimisations; the first build compiles PyO3 too, ~10 s):

import subprocess

out = subprocess.run(
    ["maturin", "develop", "--release", "--manifest-path", "_files/integ_rs/Cargo.toml"],
    capture_output=True, text=True,
)
print((out.stderr or out.stdout)[-400:])
out.check_returncode()

Profiling
You should really profile before optimising – here it comes after only because you have now seen the code. Profiling answers “where does the time (or memory) actually go?”, which is usually not where you would guess.

cProfile – function-level

import cProfile, pstats, io

pr = cProfile.Profile()
pr.enable()
primes1(200)
pr.disable()

buf = io.StringIO()
pstats.Stats(pr, stream=buf).sort_stats("cumulative").print_stats(6)
print(buf.getvalue())

         43 function calls in 0.001 seconds

   Ordered by: cumulative time
   List reduced from 20 to 6 due to restriction <6>

   ncalls  tottime  percall  cumtime  percall filename:lineno(function)
        2    0.000    0.000    0.001    0.000 /Users/vitvly/c/lnu/md/data_analytics/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/IPython/core/interactiveshell.py:3786(run_code)
        2    0.000    0.000    0.001    0.000 {built-in method builtins.exec}
        1    0.001    0.001    0.001    0.001 /var/folders/d4/0b32xzkd12gcwpwf2dqwdht80000gn/T/ipykernel_36919/2011623162.py:1(primes1)
        1    0.000    0.000    0.000    0.000 /var/folders/d4/0b32xzkd12gcwpwf2dqwdht80000gn/T/ipykernel_36919/3079768346.py:1(<module>)
        1    0.000    0.000    0.000    0.000 {method 'disable' of '_lsprof.Profiler' objects}
        2    0.000    0.000    0.000    0.000 /opt/homebrew/Cellar/python@3.14/3.14.7/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.14/lib/python3.14/codeop.py:112(__call__)





Top of the list is where the cumulative time sits. Interactively you would just write %prun primes1(200); the explicit form above is used here because %prun sends its report to a pager that a non-interactive render swallows.


line_profiler – line-by-line
uv add line_profiler

from line_profiler import LineProfiler

lp = LineProfiler()
lp.add_function(integrate_f)
lp.runcall(lambda: df.apply(lambda r: integrate_f(r["a"], r["b"], r["N"]), axis=1))

buf = io.StringIO()
lp.print_stats(stream=buf)
print(buf.getvalue())

Timer unit: 1e-09 s

Total time: 0.298537 s
File: /var/folders/d4/0b32xzkd12gcwpwf2dqwdht80000gn/T/ipykernel_36919/732619065.py
Function: integrate_f at line 5

Line #      Hits         Time  Per Hit   % Time  Line Contents
==============================================================
     5                                           def integrate_f(a, b, N):
     6      1000     190000.0    190.0      0.1      s = 0
     7      1000     196000.0    196.0      0.1      dx = (b - a) / N
     8    541117   72084000.0    133.2     24.1      for i in range(N):
     9    540117  225921000.0    418.3     75.7          s += f(a + i * dx)
    10      1000     146000.0    146.0      0.0      return s * dx




The % Time column pins the cost to a single line – the for i in range(N) loop – which is exactly what the Cython / Numba versions target. Interactively this is %load_ext line_profiler then %lprun -f integrate_f ....


%memit – peak memory of an expression
uv add memory_profiler

import sys
%load_ext memory_profiler
%memit big_list = [0] * 10_000_000
print("list overhead :", sys.getsizeof(big_list) / 1e6, "MB of pointers")
print("ndarray nbytes:", np.zeros(10_000_000, dtype="int64").nbytes / 1e6, "MB, contiguous")

peak memory: 361.58 MiB, increment: 76.75 MiB
list overhead : 80.000056 MB of pointers
ndarray nbytes: 80.0 MB, contiguous


%memit reports the peak memory of the expression: ~76 MiB just to hold 10 million pointers to the same cached 0. The equivalent int64 array is 80 MB in one contiguous block – same element count, but the cache can stream it.


scalene – CPU + GPU + memory, and where the time goes
uv add scalene
scalene is a sampling profiler with low overhead (~10–20%). Its report is a browser UI, or a terminal table with --cli, so it does not render usefully inside a notebook – run it on a script:
scalene --cli --reduced-profile myscript.py     # terminal, significant lines only
scalene myscript.py                             # interactive HTML report
What makes it worth learning for this lab: for every line it splits the time into

Python time – interpreter overhead; the part Cython / Numba / PyO3 can remove
native time – already inside compiled C (NumPy, BLAS, …); rewriting this line will not help
system time – I/O and waiting

and alongside CPU it tracks memory over time and copy volume (MB/s copied), which catches accidental copies – np.array(some_list) in a loop, a pandas .copy() you did not mean, df[mask] in a hot path.






TipReading it




a line that is ~95% native time is not your problem – it is already fast C
a line that is ~90% Python time inside a loop is exactly what you port to Cython / Numba / Rust
a line with high copy volume is an allocation to hoist out of the loop









NoteOther tools




%mprun – line-by-line memory (needs the function in an importable file)
py-spy – sampling profiler that attaches to an already-running process, no code changes: py-spy top --pid <PID>, py-spy dump --pid <PID>
snakeviz – browser icicle/flame view of a saved run: python -m cProfile -o out.prof script.py && snakeviz out.prof
viztracer – full execution timeline, viewable in Perfetto / chrome://tracing

title: Big Data Analytics: Lab 2
text:
Exercises

Apply Cython / Numba optimizations to some computations on your dataframe from Lab 1.
Go through the tutorial on Black-Scholes option pricing (https://louis-finegan.github.io/2024/10/10/Black-Scholes.html). Modify the code so that:


it works for some different company
has three versions: Cython, Numba, and PyO3
measure and compare the results


Profile primes1 (or your own slow function) with cProfile and line_profiler. Identify the single hottest line, write a faster version, and confirm with the profiler that the hotspot moved.
Add a third function to _files/integ_rs (for example the Black-Scholes formula, or a prime sieve), rebuild with maturin develop, and benchmark it against the Cython and Numba equivalents. Note how the edit/build/measure loop differs from %%cython.

title: Big Data Analytics: Lab 2
text:
Project ideas
Data-science flavoured. Pick one. In each case: start from the natural slow version (a df.apply(..., axis=1), a groupby().apply(), a rolling().apply(), or a plain Python loop), then produce at least three faster variants (NumPy-vectorised, Numba, Cython, PyO3), profile with line_profiler / scalene at each step to confirm where the time goes, and finish with a speedup table plus a paragraph on which approach was the least effort for the most gain. Reuse _files/transactions.csv and _files/depression_data.csv from Lab 1 where possible.

Row-wise feature engineering / business rules. Build a customer “risk score” or segment label from 10+ nested if/else rules with lookups and date arithmetic over transactions.csv. Baseline: df.apply(fn, axis=1). Variants: vectorised np.select / np.where; a Numba kernel over the raw column arrays; a PyO3 function taking the columns. The single most common real-world “my pandas is slow” case.
Custom group-by aggregation pandas cannot vectorise. Per-customer metrics over transactions.csv: time since previous purchase, longest fraud-free streak, a recency-weighted spend score. Baseline: groupby("customer_id").apply(py_fn). Variants: sort once, then a Numba pass over the sorted arrays; a Rust equivalent; whatever pure-pandas trick you can find.
Rolling-window features with a custom reducer. On a synthetic price / sensor series: rolling regression slope, rolling entropy, rolling max-drawdown. Baseline: series.rolling(w).apply(fn, raw=True). Variants: an explicit Numba sliding window, Cython, PyO3; compare against bottleneck / numbagg.
Pairwise similarity / nearest-neighbour from scratch. Cosine or Euclidean similarity across N rows for deduplication, a simple recommender, or k-NN (and, as a stretch, k-means – the assignment step is the same loop). Pure Python -> NumPy broadcasting (watch the memory blow-up – read scalene’s copy volume) -> blocked Numba -> PyO3. Benchmark against scipy.spatial.distance.cdist and sklearn.
Geospatial: nearest facility + radius counts. Millions of synthetic (lat, lon) points and a few hundred reference locations: for each point find the nearest reference by haversine distance, and count points within R km of each reference. Vectorised NumPy -> Numba -> PyO3. Report points/second.
Text analytics from scratch: n-gram / co-occurrence counts. Tokenise a text column and build n-gram frequencies or a word co-occurrence matrix. Pure-Python dict counting -> arrays + hashing -> Cython -> Rust (very strong here). Benchmark against sklearn.feature_extraction.text.CountVectorizer.
Bootstrap / permutation testing. B = 100_000 resamples of depression_data.csv, computing a statistic each time – a bootstrap CI for mean income by education level, or a permutation test for a group difference. The resample-and-reduce loop is embarrassingly parallel: pure Python -> NumPy -> Numba parallel=True -> PyO3 with rayon. Report resamples/second and the effective parallel speedup.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
What is Big Data?



Definition


Big Data is a set of technologies designed to store, manage and analyze data that is:

too large to fit on a single machine
while accommodating for the issue of growing discrepancy between capacity, throughput and latency.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Origins



Before the term existed



X-th century: Al-Hakam’s Great Library of Cordoba - 400 000 books (catalogue in 44 volumes) (probably orders of magnitude smaller)
As of 1481, the library at the Vatican, the largest in Europe, had around thirty-five hundred books and documents (Technological Republic)
1944: librarian Fremont Rideri: “information explosion” in library holdings (microforms)
1960s-80s: relational databases and early data warehousing emerge to manage growing, structured business data.
1975: International Conference on Very Large Data Bases (VLDBs)
1997: NASA researchers Michael Cox and David Ellsworth use the term “big data” in a paper on visualization challenges that exceed memory, disk, and even local disk capacity.
2001: Doug Laney (META Group / Gartner): “3D Data Management” (Volume, Velocity, Variety)

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Origins



Google’s papers



2003: The Google File System – a distributed filesystem for very large files across commodity hardware.
2004: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters – a programming model for parallel processing at scale.
2006: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data.







Hadoop (open-source)



Doug Cutting and Mike Cafarella build Hadoop at Yahoo!
2008: Hadoop becomes a top-level Apache project.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Origins



NoSQL, cloud, and Spark



NoSQL databases (Cassandra, MongoDB, DynamoDB) address workloads that don’t fit relational models well.
Public cloud storage (S3, ~2006 onward) makes elastic, pay-as-you-go storage mainstream.
2014: Apache Spark overtakes MapReduce as the dominant batch engine, thanks to in-memory processing.







Streaming and the lakehouse



Real-time streaming platforms (Kafka, Flink) become standard for continuously arriving data.
The lakehouse pattern blends data lake flexibility with data warehouse guarantees (e.g. Delta Lake, Iceberg).
ML/AI start relying on Big Data infrastructure

title: Big Data: Intro
text: Timeline

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Total estimate



Estimate


The total amount of data stored digitally worldwide is estimated to be getting close to 100 ZB as of 2021 (zettabytes)

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Growth trend



Future



IDC estimates the “Global Datasphere” more than doubles roughly every 4-5 years.
Machine-generated data (sensors, logs, video) is growing faster than human-generated data.
Falling storage cost per GB is part of what makes such growth economically viable.
2025 is estimated at 173.4 ZB with 2026 tracking toward 230–240 ZB, and 2029 at roughly 527 ZB

Three Vs



Volume
Variety
Velocity

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Volume



Issue


Data volume has exponentially increased in recent decades.






Wait but why?



Internet-of-Things sensor data
Social networks
Storage device progress

Types



trees - XML, JSON, Parquet, Avro, etc
unstructured - text, pictures, audio, video
data cubes

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Velocity



Definion


Speed at which data is being generated, collected, and processed.






Attributes



Capacity: how much data can we store per unit of volume?
Throughput: how many bytes can we read per unit of time?
Latency: how much time do we need to wait until the bytes start arriving?

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Velocity
Evolution since 1950s

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
More Vs: Veracity



Definition


The trustworthiness and quality of data.

Sensor noise, human error, and inconsistent formats erode veracity.
Garbage in the pipeline still means garbage out, no matter the volume.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
More Vs: Value



Definition


The usefulness extracted from data relative to the cost of storing and processing it.

Not all data is worth keeping forever.
Big Data investments are ultimately justified by the value they unlock, not by size alone.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
More Vs: Variability



Definition


How the meaning and format of data can shift over time or context.

The same field name might mean different things across systems.
Data drift can silently break assumptions made by downstream models.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
A few more Vs



Sometimes mentioned



Visualization: making sense of results is itself a challenge at scale.
Validity: is the data correct and applicable for the intended use, distinct from raw quality (Veracity)?

text:
Features



Features



Reliability
Scalability
Maintainability

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Reliability



Kleppmann’s definition


The system should continue to work correctly (performing the correct function at the desired level of performance) even in the face of adversity

hardware faults
software faults
and even human error

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Reliability



Faults


Basically, theses are things that could go wrong.
Systems that can anticipate faults are called fault-tolerant or resilient.
Fault can be defined as one component of the system deviating from the spec.






Failures


Failures occur when system stops providing services to the user.



Faults might degenerate into failures.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Reliability



Types of errors



Hardware
Software
Human

title: Big Data: Intro
text: Reliability

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Scalability



Kleppmann


As the system grows (in data volume, traffic volume, or complexity), there should be reasonable ways of dealing with that growth.
In other words, scalability is a system’s ability to cope with increased load.





Note that scalability is a multi-dimensional term. When saying “system scales well”, it’s important to state exactly along which axis.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Scalability



What is load?


Load is described by load parameters. These might include:

data set size
data write speed
data read speed
computational complexity
etc…

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Scalability



Performance


Increasing load affects performance. There are several meanings to this term:

throughput – time required to process a dataset of certain size
response time – time between sending a request and receiving a response
latency – duration of waiting for a request to be processed. Included in response time.






Performance might be more strictly defined by service level objectives (SLOs) and service level agreements (SLAs).

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Scalability



How to deal with load



vertical scaling - scaling up
horizontal scaling - scaling out
architectural changes







Elasticity


An approach to load handling whereby a system automatically adds resources in case of load increase, and can decrease resources if load decreases.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Scalability



Common wisdom



Keep your database on a single node (scale up) until scaling cost or high-availability requirements forces you to make it distributed.
Optimize code so that it can run on a single node.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Scalability



CAP theorem (Brewer, 2000; Gilbert & Lynch, 2002)


Given the following definitions:

Consistency (C): every read receives the most recent write, or an error.
Availability (A): every request receives a (non-error) response, without guarantee it contains the most recent write.
Partition tolerance (P): the system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of dropped or delayed messages between nodes.

the following holds:
A distributed system can provide at most two of the three properties at the same time – but only when a network partition is actually happening.

title: Big Data: Intro
text: The CAP triangle

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Maintainability



Kleppmann


Over time, many different people will work on the system

engineering
operations
both maintaining current behavior and adapting the system to new use cases),

and they should all be able to work on it productively.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Maintainability



Principles



Operability – make it easy for operations teams to keep the system running smoothly.
Simplicity – make it easy for new engineers to understand the system, by removing as much complexity as possible from the system.
Evolvability – Make it easy for engineers to make changes to the system in the future, adapting it for unanticipated use cases as requirements change. Also known as extensibility, modifiability, or plasticity.

Operability



Health monitoring

Philosophy of Software Design (Ousterhout)



The most fundamental problem in computer science is problem decomposition


the greatest limitation in writing software is our ability to understand the systems we are creating

Types



incidental

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Maintainability: Complexity



Incidental



Easy things can be complex. There can be complex constructs that are succinctly described, familiar, available and easy to use. That is incidental complexity.

Rich Hickey talk “Simple made easy”: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SxdOUGdseq4

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Maintainability: complexity
However: Complexity is often caused by



Accidental complexity


Moseley and Marks define complexity as accidental if it is not inherent in the problem that the software solves (as seen by the users) but arises only from the implementation.






How to remove?


By providing proper abstractions.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Maintainability: abstractions






Definition (Ousterhout)


An abstraction is a simplified view of an entity, which omits unimportant details.
In modular programming, each module provides an abstraction in the form of its interface.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Maintainability: abstractions






What can abstractions do?



Hide implementation details
Provide reusable building blocks

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Maintainability



Evolvability


One needs to adapt their big data system to possible future requirements changes.
However, keep in mind the following:

Inability to foresee exact nature of changes
Need to strike the balance of flexibility and fitness for a particular task

Diagnostic

Predictive

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Batch processing



Definition


Processing a bounded, finite dataset as a single job.

High throughput, higher latency (minutes to hours).
Simple to reason about: same input always gives the same output.
Example flavor: nightly ETL jobs, end-of-day reporting.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Stream processing



Definition


Processing an unbounded sequence of events as they arrive.

Low latency (milliseconds to seconds), continuous computation.
Must handle out-of-order and late-arriving events.
Example flavor: fraud detection, real-time dashboards, alerting.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Batch vs. stream



Aspect
Batch
Stream




Data
bounded
unbounded


Latency
high
low


Throughput
high
variable


Complexity
lower
higher


Typical use
reporting, training
monitoring, alerting

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Which to choose?



Rule of thumb



Need a fresh answer within seconds? Stream.
Need to crunch the full history accurately? Batch.
Need both? Lambda/Kappa/etc.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Lambda architecture



Idea (Nathan Marz)


Run both a batch and a speed (stream) layer, then merge results in a serving layer:

Batch layer: recomputes accurate views over all historical data.
Speed layer: provides low-latency approximate views over recent data.
Serving layer: merges both for queries.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Lambda architecture: tradeoffs



The catch



Every piece of logic must be implemented twice – once for batch, once for streaming.
Keeping the two implementations consistent is a real maintenance burden.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Kappa architecture



Idea (Jay Kreps)


Treat everything as a stream, including historical data (replayed through the same pipeline).

One code path instead of two.
Reprocessing = replaying the stream from an earlier offset.
Requires a log that can retain and replay history (e.g. Kafka-style).

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Lambda vs. Kappa



Summary



Lambda: proven, flexible, but duplicated logic.
Kappa: simpler mental model, but depends on your streaming platform being able to replay history efficiently.

text: Lambda vs. Kappa

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Challenges






Challenges



how do we store and manage such a huge volume of data efficiently?
how do we process and extract valuable information from the data within the given time frame?

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Storage & management



What makes it hard?



data volume outpaces the growth of storage capacity per node
redundancy needed for fault tolerance multiplies storage cost
choosing the wrong format or layout wastes both space and query performance

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Processing within a time frame



What makes it hard?



some questions need answers in milliseconds, others can wait hours
picking the wrong paradigm (batch vs. stream) wastes either latency or resources
computation itself has a cost

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Data quality & integration



What makes it hard?



combining sources with different schemas, units, and conventions
missing, duplicate, or inconsistent records (Veracity, revisited)
“garbage in, garbage out” applies at any scale

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Skills & organization



What makes it hard?



demand for skilled data engineers and scientists has long outpaced supply
Maintainability (from earlier) is a people problem as much as a technical one
engineering, analytics, and ML teams often want different things from the same data

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Cost management



What makes it hard?



cloud storage/compute bills scale with data volume – easy to underestimate
Value (one of the extended Vs) has to justify that cost, or the pipeline isn’t worth running
over-provisioning “just in case” is a common and expensive habit

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Security & privacy



What makes it hard?



more data concentrated in one place is a bigger target
access control gets harder as more teams need access to the same data

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Healthcare



Examples



Genomic sequencing pipelines process terabytes per patient.
Medical imaging (MRI/CT) archives at population scale.
Real-time monitoring in ICUs generates continuous sensor streams.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Finance



Examples



Fraud detection on card transactions, scored in milliseconds.
Algorithmic trading reacting to market data streams.
Risk modeling over years of historical transaction data.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Retail & e-commerce



Examples



Recommendation engines built from clickstream and purchase history.
Demand forecasting and inventory optimization.
Dynamic pricing driven by real-time competitor and demand signals.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Social media



Examples



Feed ranking over billions of daily interactions.
Ad targeting from behavioral and interest data.
Content moderation at a scale no human team could review manually.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
IoT & sensors



Examples



Industrial equipment emitting continuous telemetry for predictive maintenance.
Smart grids balancing electricity supply and demand in real time.
Connected vehicles streaming location and diagnostic data.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Science & geospatial



Examples



Satellite and remote-sensing imagery archives (petabyte-scale).
Climate and weather simulation output.
We’ll spend several lectures later in this course on geospatial Big Data specifically.

title: Big Data: Intro
text: Ecosystem

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Ecosystem



Categories



Compute & scaling: multi-core, GPU, and cluster techniques for speeding up computation.
Fast dataframes: single-node engines that outrun pandas without going distributed.
Distributed/parallel processing frameworks: tools like Dask that spread work across cores and machines.
Storage & table formats: how data is laid out on disk, and how ACID guarantees get layered on top of it.
Databases & query engines: systems for querying large structured datasets, locally or across a cluster.
Orchestration & streaming: scheduling pipelines, and handling data that never stops arriving.
ML tooling: tracking, serving, and scaling machine learning on top of all of the above.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Columnar storage



Row vs. column layout



Row-oriented formats (CSV, JSON) store a record’s fields together – good for reading whole rows.
Columnar formats (Parquet, ORC) store each column together – good for reading a few columns out of many, and for compression.
Analytical (“OLAP”) workloads scan a handful of columns over huge tables, so columnar storage dominates the Big Data world.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Apache Arrow



A shared in-memory format


Arrow defines a columnar, in-memory layout that many tools agree on.

Data can move between Pandas, Polars, DuckDB, Spark, and others without copying or re-serializing it.
It’s a big reason today’s “fast dataframe” tools interoperate so easily.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Fast, single-node dataframes



Why?


Pandas is single-threaded and loads everything into RAM. A newer generation of tools targets the same “fits on one machine, but not comfortably in pandas” gap:

multi-threaded execution
lazy, optimized query plans
Arrow-native memory layout

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Polars



Rust-powered dataframes



Implemented in Rust, exposes a Python (and Rust) API.
Multi-threaded by default, unlike pandas.
Offers a lazy API: build a query plan, let an optimizer rewrite it, then execute.
Built on the Arrow memory format.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
DuckDB



“SQLite for analytics”



An in-process, embeddable OLAP SQL database – no server to run.
Can query Parquet, CSV, and Arrow data directly, including files sitting in cloud storage.
Vectorized, columnar execution engine tuned for analytical queries over local files.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
GPU & out-of-core dataframes



More flavors of “faster than pandas”

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Table formats: the lakehouse idea



The problem


A folder of Parquet files on cheap storage is fast and cheap – but has no transactions, no schema enforcement, and no easy way to update or delete rows.






The fix


Table formats – Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, Apache Hudi – add a metadata layer on top of plain files to bring ACID transactions, schema evolution, and time travel to a data lake.

title: Big Data: Intro
text:
Lakehouse architecture



Putting it together



Storage: cheap object storage (S3-style), holding columnar files.
Table format: Iceberg/Delta/Hudi metadata, giving ACID guarantees over those files.
Query engine: something that reads the table format and runs SQL over it.

The result is called a lakehouse: warehouse-style guarantees on lake-style storage.

The idea


Instead of hand-writing pipeline code, describe transformations as SQL select statements and let the tool compile them into a dependency-ordered set of queries run by your warehouse or engine.

Models can reference each other; the tool builds a DAG and runs everything in the correct order.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Query languages: SQL



Example


SELECT c.century AS cent,
       COUNT(c.name) AS num_captains,
       SUM(s.id) AS ships
FROM captains c, ships s
WHERE c.id = s.captain
GROUP BY century
HAVING COUNT(c.name) >= 3
ORDER BY century DESC
LIMIT 3 OFFSET 2

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
SQL



Clauses



The FROM clause selects from which tables to read the data, in this case two tables, captains and ships. Implicitly the Cartesian product is computed.
The WHERE clause performs a selection: it only keeps the records for which the captain (from the captains table) is the captain of the ship (from the ships table). If you pay attention, you will recognize that this filter together with the Cartesian product is actually a theta join. Any reasonable SQL implementation will be smart enough to detect this and evaluate this query efficiently (joins can be computed in linear time rather than quadratic!).
The SELECT clause is also where projections are made: it lists the columns to include in the results. Renames are also made in this clause with AS.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
SQL



Clauses



The GROUP BY clause performs an aggregation, with century as a grouping key. Aggregations on the captain name (COUNT) and the ship id (SUM) are done in the SELECT clause.
The HAVING clause is in fact like the WHERE clause, but performs a selection after, rather than before, the grouping.
The ORDER BY clause reorders the output rows according to the specified keys.
The LIMIT and OFFSET clauses allow pagination of the output: OFFSET specifies how many records to skip, and LIMIT specifies how many records to output after the skipped ones.
All clauses are optional except for SELECT and FROM.

Query languages: Cypher



Cypher vs SQL: find


WITH RECURSIVE
  -- in_usa is the set of vertex IDs of all locations within the United States
  in_usa(vertex_id) AS (
    SELECT vertex_id FROM vertices WHERE properties->>'name' = 'United States'
    UNION
    SELECT edges.tail_vertex FROM edges
    JOIN in_usa ON edges.head_vertex = in_usa.vertex_id
    WHERE edges.label = 'within'
  ),
  -- in_europe is the set of vertex IDs of all locations within Europe
  in_europe(vertex_id) AS (
    SELECT vertex_id FROM vertices WHERE properties->>'name' = 'Europe'
    UNION
    SELECT edges.tail_vertex FROM edges
    JOIN in_europe ON edges.head_vertex = in_europe.vertex_id
    WHERE edges.label = 'within'
  ),
  -- born_in_usa is the set of vertex IDs of all people born in the US
  born_in_usa(vertex_id) AS (
    SELECT edges.tail_vertex FROM edges
    JOIN in_usa ON edges.head_vertex = in_usa.vertex_id
    WHERE edges.label = 'born_in'
  ),
  -- lives_in_europe is the set of vertex IDs of all people living in Europe
  lives_in_europe(vertex_id) AS (
    SELECT edges.tail_vertex FROM edges
    JOIN in_europe ON edges.head_vertex = in_europe.vertex_id
    WHERE edges.label = 'lives_in'
  )
  SELECT vertices.properties->>'name'
  FROM vertices
  -- join to find those people who were both born in the US *and* live in Europe
  JOIN born_in_usa ON vertices.vertex_id = born_in_usa.vertex_id
  JOIN lives_in_europe ON vertices.vertex_id = lives_in_europe.vertex_id;

Definition


A Datalog program is a collection of Datalog rules, each of which is of the form: \[
A :- B_1,B_2,\ldots,B_n,
\] where \(n \geq 0\), A is the head of the rule, and the conjunction of \(B_1,\ldots,B_n\) is the body of the rule.
The rule can be read informally as “\(B_1\) and \(B_2\) and \(\ldots\) and \(B_n\) implies \(A\)”.

Storage engines: logs



Definition


Sorted string table (SSTable): sort key-value entries by key.
Advantages:

Merge is faster
No need to keep hashes for all entries
Records can be grouped into blocks and compressed

Introduced in Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data, Google (2006).

text:
Storage engines: logs



How to sort data on disk?



When a write comes in, add it to an in-memory balanced tree data structure (a memtable)
When the memtable gets bigger than some threshold—typically a few megabytes —write it out to disk as an SSTable file.
In order to serve a read request, first try to find the key in the memtable, then in the most recent on-disk segment, then in the next-older segment, etc.
From time to time, run a merging and compaction process in the background

Log-Structured Merge-Tree


LSM-tree: introduced in The Log-Structured Merge-Tree, Patrick O’Neil et al. (1996).
Storage engines that are based on this principle of merging and compacting sorted files are often called LSM storage engines.
Basic idea: keeping a cascade of SSTables that are merged in the background.

Storage engines: logs



Performance optimizations



Use Bloom filters for segment checks
size-tiered compaction: newer and smaller SSTables are successively merged into older and larger SSTables.
leveled compaction: the key range is split up into smaller SSTables and older data is moved into separate “levels,” which allows the compaction to proceed more incrementally and use less disk space.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Storage engines: trees



B-trees


Introduced in Organization and Maintenance of Large Ordered Indices, Bayer et al, Boeing Scientific Research Laboratories, 1970.

B-trees break the database down into fixed-size blocks or pages, traditionally 4 KB in size (sometimes bigger), and read or write one page at a time.
Each page contains several keys and references to child pages.
Number of references to child pages in one page of the B-tree is called the branching factor.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Storage engines: trees



Definition


Let \(h \geq 0\) be an integer, \(k\) a natural number. A directed tree \(T\) is in the class \(\tau(k,h)\) of B-trees if \(T\) is either empty (\(h=0\)) or has the following properties:

Each path from the root to any leaf has the same length \(h\), also called the height of \(T\), i.e., \(h\) = number of nodes in path.
Each node except the root and the leaves has at least \(k + 1\) sons. The root is a leaf or has at least two sons.
Each node has at most \(2k + 1\) sons.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Storage engines: trees



B-tree Update



search for the leaf page containing that key
change the value in that page
write the page back to disk (any references to that page remain valid)







B-tree Insert



find the page whose range encompasses the new key
add it to that page.
If there isn’t enough free space in the page to accommodate the new key, it is split into two half-full pages, and the parent page is updated to account for the new subdivision of key ranges

text:
Storage engines: trees



Balancing


This algorithm ensures that the tree remains balanced:

a B-tree with \(n\) keys always has a depth of \(O(\log n)\)
most databases can fit into a B-tree that is three or four levels deep
four-level tree of 4 KB pages with a branching factor of 500 can store up to 256 TB.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Storage engines: trees



B-tree optimizations



write-ahead log (WAL). This is an append-only file to which every B-tree modification must be written before it can be applied to the pages of the tree itself.
latches (lightweight locks): solve concurrency issues by protecting the tree’s data structures
copy-on-write for new page creation
key abbreviation. Especially in pages on the interior of the tree, keys only need to provide enough information to act as boundaries between key ranges. Packing more keys into a page allows the tree to have a higher branching factor, and thus fewer levels
additional tree pointers, e.g. siblings

LSM-trees are typically faster for writes
B-trees are thought to be faster for reads
Compaction process interferes with ongoing read/write performance
LSM-trees: lower storage overhead
LSM-trees: issue of write amplification
B-trees: each key exists exactly in one place in the index

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Seven steps


Provenance and structure — where did this come from, and what shape is it in?
Measurement — what do the values measure, and what does absence mean?
Estimand — what number am I trying to learn, and what makes it identifiable?
Estimation — which estimator, and why that one?
Uncertainty — how wrong could this be, and from how many sources?
Evaluation — how would I know if it were wrong?
Delivery — can someone else get this number again, and who acts on it?
