title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Step 0 — Framing
The rubric starts at Step 1 with a dataset already in hand. That is a real gap. Nothing in the seven steps asks whether this is the right question.

CoNVO, from Shron’s Thinking with Data — written before a dataset is chosen:

Context — whose problem is this, and what are they trying to achieve?
Need — what is broken that this fixes? A deficiency in the world, not a request for a technique.
Vision — a sketch of the finished artefact.
Outcome — how it gets used, and how you would know a year later that it mattered.



Then the mockup: draw the final figure, with invented numbers, before touching data. If you cannot draw it, you do not yet know what the project is.


This is the same discipline as estimand-before-estimator, one level up. Left to themselves students propose a dataset and a method, which is backwards, and the error stays invisible until the project fails in week 15.
The mockup is the item to enforce hardest in the week 9 proposal. Fifteen minutes with a pen versus a failed capstone.
Say plainly that CoNVO is not a substitute for an identification argument — Shron’s causality chapter is thin and weeks 2 to 4 supersede it.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
An analysis is an argument
Shron imports Toulmin’s structure. It maps onto the spine almost cell for cell.









Toulmin
Spine
In practice




Claim
3–4
The estimate


Evidence
1–2
The data, and what it measures


Warrant
3
The identification assumptions


Backing
3
Why you believe the warrant: DAG, mechanism, domain knowledge


Qualifier
5
The uncertainty, from all its sources


Rebuttal
5–6
Falsification, negative controls, sensitivity analysis





Conditional exchangeability is a warrant: the unstated bridge that licenses moving from evidence to claim, and the first thing an opponent attacks.


An untestable assumption is not a defect of the method. It is the load-bearing element of the argument.


This slide is for the students who find the formalism alienating. It gives them a rhetorical vocabulary for the thing the spine does statistically, and the warrant row is the one that changes how they read papers.
It also sharpens peer review in week 16: “which warrant is weakest, and what backing would strengthen it” beats “critique this analysis” by a wide margin.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
The question

Where did these numbers come from, who produced them, why, and what did they gain or lose by producing them? And what shape is the result in?


Two concerns, one work session: you read the codebook, load the data, model the schema, and write the validation rules in a single sitting.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Data are not found objects
Someone chose an instrument, a sampling frame, a coding scheme, a retention policy, and a release schedule — usually for reasons unrelated to your analysis.


Administrative data exist to run a process, not to be analysed. Categories change when the process changes.
Survey data carry a design: strata, clusters, weights. Ignoring it gives wrong point estimates and badly wrong standard errors.
Sensor data carry an instrument: calibration drift, saturation, missing scans.
Derived data carry someone else’s model, with its own assumptions baked in.



The reanalysis products in week 5 are the clearest case of the last one: ERA5 is not observation, it is a physical model constrained by observation. Students who treat it as ground truth will over-trust it in exactly the regions where observations are sparse.

title: Applied Data Analytics
section: Five questions, in writing, every project
text:
Five questions, in writing, every project


What is the unit of observation, precisely?
What is the target population, and how does the sampling frame differ from it?
What was measured, and what was derived, imputed, or modelled upstream?
Has this been revised since publication, and does the archive keep the vintage you need?
If someone had an incentive to influence these numbers, how would they do it?



These are graded. A project that answers them badly cannot recover in later steps.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Question 2, elaborated: frame versus population
The sampling frame is what you can draw from. The target population is what you want to speak about. They are never the same.










Domain
Frame
Population
Gap




Astronomy
Bright, nearby objects
All objects
Malmquist bias


Genomics
European-ancestry cohorts
Humans
Portability failure of PGS


Healthcare
Patients who presented
People with the condition
Berkson-type selection


NLP
Documents a platform retained
Discourse
Moderation and deletion





In week 6 you will estimate the astronomy version of this gap directly, by injecting synthetic signals and counting recoveries.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Question 4, elaborated: vintages
Macroeconomic series are revised. Fundamental data are restated. Satellite archives are reprocessed. Clinical codes are back-filled.

Using the final vintage when your analysis would have seen the initial release is a silent and severe error. FRED’s ALFRED archive exists precisely to make this checkable.


The general rule: point-in-time data. What was knowable, when.


This is the look-ahead bias problem in week 9 and it recurs in energy forecasting in week 13 as the weather-forecast-versus-weather-actual distinction. Flag the connection now.

title: Applied Data Analytics
section: Structure: schema is a modelling decision
text:
Structure: schema is a modelling decision
You already know SQL, so this moves fast. Given three incompatible sources, what is the right target schema — and what does “right” mean here?


Dimensional modelling; entity-relationship reasoning over messy sources
What is an entity and what is an attribute (a judgement with real consequences)
Tidy long format versus wide analysis matrix, and when to move between them
Schema evolution: what happens when a source adds a column



And the one most people have never met:

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Valid time versus transaction time

Valid time — when the fact was true in the world.
Transaction time — when your database learned it.



What did we believe about this supplier’s ownership on the date the contract was awarded?



A non-bitemporal warehouse cannot answer that question. Every audit, compliance, and backtesting application needs it.


This is week 11 material but plant it now. Snodgrass is free online and is the best treatment. The connection to point-in-time financial data on the previous slide is exact: they are the same idea discovered independently by two communities.

title: Applied Data Analytics
section: Contracts: validation that fails, not warns
text:
Contracts: validation that fails, not warns
import pandera as pa

schema = pa.DataFrameSchema({
    "patient_id":  pa.Column(str, unique=True),
    "admit_date":  pa.Column("datetime64[ns]"),
    "discharge":   pa.Column("datetime64[ns]", nullable=True),
    "age":         pa.Column(int, pa.Check.in_range(0, 120)),
}, checks=pa.Check(lambda df: (df.discharge >= df.admit_date).all()))

A schema test checks types and ranges. A semantic test checks that the data mean something coherent — discharge after admission, weights summing to a population, a hierarchy that actually nests.


Both belong in the pipeline, and both should stop it.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Step 0 and Step 1 — references

Shron, M. (2014). Thinking with Data: How to Turn Information into Insights. O’Reilly. — CoNVO, mockups, and the argument structure. Short.
Toulmin, S. E. (1958/2003). The Uses of Argument. Cambridge University Press.
Klein, G. (2007). Performing a project premortem. Harvard Business Review.
Gebru, T., Morgenstern, J., Vecchione, B., et al. (2021). Datasheets for datasets. Communications of the ACM 64(12).
Leek, J. T., and Peng, R. D. (2015). What is the question? Science 347(6228).
Lumley, T. (2010). Complex Surveys: A Guide to Analysis Using R. Wiley. — for the survey design material.
Snodgrass, R. T. (1999). Developing Time-Oriented Database Applications in SQL. Morgan Kaufmann. Freely available from the author.
Kimball, R., and Ross, M. (2013). The Data Warehouse Toolkit, 3rd ed. Wiley.
Chapman, P., et al. (1999). CRISP-DM 1.0: Step-by-step data mining guide.
Wilson, G., Bryan, J., Cranston, K., et al. (2017). Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology 13(6).

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
The question

What do the recorded values actually measure, and what does absence mean?


This is where most of you are weakest, because undergraduate data arrives pre-cleaned.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Absence is a measurement

A laboratory value is absent because nobody ordered the test.
Nobody ordered the test because the clinician was not worried.
The clinician’s worry is what you are trying to predict.


The missingness is more informative than the value.


Add an indicator for whether each test was ordered and predictive performance jumps. Then ask what happens when the hospital changes its ordering protocol.


That last question is the whole lesson. The indicator is real signal and it is also a dependency on an institutional practice that can change overnight. This is week 8 and it recurs in week 12 as implicit feedback.

title: Applied Data Analytics
section: MCAR, MAR, MNAR — and the limits
text:
MCAR, MAR, MNAR — and the limits

MCAR — missingness independent of everything. Almost never true; testable in principle.


MAR — missingness depends only on observed data. This is what multiple imputation requires, and it is not testable from the data you have.


MNAR — missingness depends on the unobserved value itself. Imputation is invalid; you need a model of the missingness mechanism or you need bounds.


The taxonomy’s real limitation: MAR versus MNAR is an assumption about a mechanism, and no diagnostic distinguishes them. Argue for it, do not test for it.

title: Applied Data Analytics
section: The same problem in three domains
text:
The same problem in three domains









Domain
Absence means
Naive treatment
Consequence




Healthcare
Test not ordered
Impute the mean
Erases the clinician’s judgement


Recommenders
Item not clicked
Treat as negative
Confounds exposure with preference


Knowledge graphs
Edge not asserted
Treat as false
Closed-world assumption, silently




Three literatures, one problem: the absence of a record is being read as evidence of absence.


This slide ties weeks 8, 11 and 12 together and it is worth dwelling on. The knowledge-graph row is the crispest formal statement, because the KR tradition named the assumption explicitly and the other two communities did not.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Measurement error: two kinds

Classical. \(X_{obs} = X_{true} + \varepsilon\), with \(\varepsilon\) independent of \(X_{true}\). In simple regression this attenuates the coefficient toward zero. Students find this reassuring and then over-generalise it.


Berkson. \(X_{true} = X_{obs} + \varepsilon\) — the assigned or group-level value is the observed one, and individual deviation is the error. Occurs with dose assignment, area-level exposure, and any group-mean proxy. It does not attenuate.


With multiple mismeasured covariates, the direction of bias is not predictable at all. “Attenuation means my estimate is conservative” is false in general.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Construct validity
Does the proxy measure the concept?


Nightlights as a proxy for economic activity
Clicks as a proxy for preference
Test scores as a proxy for learning
Publication counts as a proxy for research quality
Expected goals as a proxy for chance quality



Two ways to validate a construct you cannot observe: convergent (does it agree with an independent measure of the same thing?) and criterion (does it predict something it should predict?).


In week 10 you will build a construct from scratch and measure how well humans agree with each other about it before asking whether a model agrees with humans.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Censoring and truncation are different

Censoring — the unit is in your sample, but the value is only bounded. A drive that has not failed by the end of observation has survived at least that long.


Truncation — the unit is not in your sample at all, because of its value. Objects fainter than the detection limit simply do not appear.


Dropping censored units biases you. Treating them as negative outcomes biases you differently and worse. Week 15 is built on this.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Step 2 — references

Little, R. J. A., and Rubin, D. B. (2019). Statistical Analysis with Missing Data, 3rd ed. Wiley.
van Buuren, S. (2018). Flexible Imputation of Missing Data, 2nd ed. Freely available online. — the practical companion.
Carroll, R. J., Ruppert, D., Stefanski, L. A., and Crainiceanu, C. M. (2006). Measurement Error in Nonlinear Models, 2nd ed. Chapman & Hall/CRC.
Klein, J. P., and Moeschberger, M. L. (2003). Survival Analysis: Techniques for Censored and Truncated Data, 2nd ed. Springer.
Manski, C. F. (2003). Partial Identification of Probability Distributions. Springer. — for what to do when you cannot assume your way out.
Jacobs, A. Z., and Wallach, H. (2021). Measurement and fairness. FAccT. — construct validity, stated for a computational audience.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
The question

What number am I trying to learn, defined without reference to any estimation procedure?


Twenty percent of the capstone. The largest single weight in the rubric.


A model can predict beautifully on the world as it is and be arbitrarily wrong about the world as it would be under intervention. \(P(Y \mid X)\) and \(P(Y \mid do(X))\) coincide only under conditions you must argue for and can never observe.

title: Applied Data Analytics
section: The sentence you must write first
text:
The sentence you must write first


I want to estimate the average change in \(Y\) that would result from setting \(X\) from \(x_0\) to \(x_1\), in population \(P\), at time \(t\).



You are forbidden from writing code until this sentence exists.


Only then does the question of method arise. This discipline comes from the clinical trials literature — ICH E9(R1) — and it is the single most valuable habit this course can give you.


Enforce this literally in the first problem set. Require the sentence at the top of the submission. It feels bureaucratic for two weeks and then becomes automatic.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Potential outcomes
For unit \(i\) and binary treatment \(A_i \in \{0,1\}\), define \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\): what would be observed under each treatment.
\[Y_i = A_i Y_i(1) + (1 - A_i) Y_i(0)\]

Exactly one is ever observed.


Holland’s fundamental problem: causal inference is a missing data problem where half the data are missing by construction.


Mathematics students take to this quickly. The difficulty is never technical — it is that the central object is not defined in terms of data, and they are unused to a quantity no dataset contains.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Which average?




Estimand
Definition
When you want it




ATE
\(E[Y(1) - Y(0)]\)
Universal policy


ATT
\(E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid A = 1]\)
Should we have done what we did?


CATE
\(E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]\)
Targeting, personalisation


LATE
Effect among compliers
What an instrument gives you





These differ, often substantially. Confusing them is common and consequential.


In week 7 you will estimate a LATE via Mendelian randomisation and have to argue about whether the complier subpopulation is the one anyone cares about.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Three assumptions

1. Consistency / SUTVA. The observed outcome is the potential outcome under the received treatment, and one unit’s treatment does not affect another’s. Interference violates the second half — pervasive in networks, epidemics, markets, and electricity grids.


2. Conditional exchangeability. \(\{Y(1), Y(0)\} \perp A \mid X\). This does the work. It is never testable. Everything in the design of an observational study is an argument for it.


3. Positivity. \(0 < P(A = 1 \mid X = x) < 1\). Unlike the second, this is checkable — plot the propensity distribution by arm, every time.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Graphs: the three structures
CONFOUNDER          COLLIDER            MEDIATOR

    L                   A                   A
   / \                   \                   \
  v   v                   v                   v
  A-->Y               C <--                   M
                     ^                         \
                    Y                           v
                                                Y

Adjust for the confounder. Do not adjust for the collider — conditioning on a common effect creates association where none existed. Do not adjust for the mediator if you want the total effect.


The collider case must be taught with a simulation, not an argument. Four lines: generate two independent variables, select on their sum exceeding a threshold, compute the correlation in the selected subsample. It comes out strongly negative and the magnitude surprises people.
“Among survivors”, “among hospitalised patients”, “among funded startups”, “among published studies” are all this.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
The back-door criterion
A set \(Z\) suffices to identify the effect of \(A\) on \(Y\) if it blocks every back-door path and contains no descendant of \(A\).

This turns “which variables should I control for?” from a matter of taste into a question with a defensible answer given stated assumptions.


Mechanise it: dagitty or DoWhy will enumerate valid adjustment sets from a graph you draw. The work is in drawing the graph honestly.


The folk rule “adjust for everything you have” is wrong. So is “adjust for everything pre-treatment” — see M-bias.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Designs you will meet

Benchmark

Healthcare (wk 8)


Difference-in-differences

Weighted donors reproduce pre-trend

Instrumental variables

Energy (wk 13)

Recommenders (wk 12)





Note the last row. It is the only setting where the propensity score is recorded rather than estimated, which makes it an unusually clean teaching case.


If your problem is genuinely predictive, you still owe an equivalent: what is the deployment distribution, what decision does the prediction support, and what is the cost asymmetry? “Maximise AUC” is not an estimand — it is an abdication of Step 3.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Step 3 — references

Hernán, M. A., and Robins, J. M. Causal Inference: What If. Chapman & Hall/CRC. Freely available. Chapter 1 is assigned for next week.
Pearl, J. (2009). Causality: Models, Reasoning, and Inference, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.
Holland, P. W. (1986). Statistics and causal inference. JASA 81(396).
Elwert, F., and Winship, C. (2014). Endogenous selection bias: the problem of conditioning on a collider variable. Annual Review of Sociology 40.
Westreich, D., and Greenland, S. (2013). The Table 2 fallacy. American Journal of Epidemiology 177(4).
Textor, J., van der Zander, B., et al. (2016). Robust causal inference using directed acyclic graphs: the R package dagitty. IJE 45(6).
ICH (2019). E9(R1) Addendum on Estimands and Sensitivity Analysis in Clinical Trials.
Cunningham, S. (2021). Causal Inference: The Mixtape. Yale University Press; free online.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
The question

Given the estimand and the identification argument, which estimator — and why that one?


Ten percent of the rubric. The shortest block in this lecture.


You arrive over-weighting this step. The design deliberately deflates it.

title: Applied Data Analytics
section: Regression as adjustment is not regression as prediction
text:
Regression as adjustment is not regression as prediction
Same arithmetic. Different object.

As prediction: you want \(\hat{E}[Y \mid X]\) to be accurate out of sample. Regularise freely. Include whatever helps.


As adjustment: you want one coefficient to carry a causal interpretation. Functional form misspecification biases it. Variable selection must follow the graph, not the fit.


And the coefficient on a control variable is not itself interpretable as an effect. This is the Table 2 fallacy and it is everywhere in the applied literature.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Regularisation breaks inference

A LASSO coefficient is a biased, non-linear, data-dependent quantity with no standard sampling distribution.


It is not an estimate of anything in particular, and the naive confidence interval around it does not cover.


If you need both selection and inference, use tools built for it: double machine learning with cross-fitting, or post-selection inference. Do not report LASSO coefficients with p-values.


Chernozhukov et al. (2018) is the reference. The Neyman-orthogonality plus cross-fitting construction is genuinely elegant and this audience will appreciate it in week 8.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Doubly robust estimation
Consistent if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correct.
\[\hat{\tau}_{AIPW} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \left[ \hat{\mu}_1(X_i) - \hat{\mu}_0(X_i) + \frac{A_i(Y_i - \hat{\mu}_1(X_i))}{\hat{e}(X_i)} - \frac{(1-A_i)(Y_i - \hat{\mu}_0(X_i))}{1 - \hat{e}(X_i)} \right]\]

Two chances to be right instead of one. The machinery — influence functions, cross-fitting — connects directly to theory you have already seen.


It is the modern default, and EconML implements it approachably.


But with poor overlap, a flexible outcome model quietly extrapolates into regions with no comparable units. The estimator should follow from the identification argument, not from a leaderboard — that sentence is the whole grading criterion for this step.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Step 4 — references

Rosenbaum, P. R., and Rubin, D. B. (1983). The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects. Biometrika 70(1).
Robins, J. M., Hernán, M. A., and Brumback, B. (2000). Marginal structural models and causal inference in epidemiology. Epidemiology 11(5).
Chernozhukov, V., Chetverikov, D., Demirer, M., et al. (2018). Double/debiased machine learning for treatment and structural parameters. The Econometrics Journal 21(1).
Wager, S., and Athey, S. (2018). Estimation and inference of heterogeneous treatment effects using random forests. JASA 113(523).
Athey, S., and Imbens, G. W. (2019). Machine learning methods that economists should know about. Annual Review of Economics 11.
Austin, P. C. (2011). An introduction to propensity score methods. Multivariate Behavioral Research 46(3).

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
The question

How wrong could this be, and from how many sources?


You arrive with Bayesian machinery, which is an advantage. The gap is elsewhere.

title: Applied Data Analytics
section: Sampling variability is the smallest source
text:
Sampling variability is the smallest source

In most applied work, the standard error is the least of your problems.



Specification uncertainty — which of forty defensible models did you fit?
Search uncertainty — how many did you try before this one?
Measurement uncertainty — how good is the proxy?
Cleaning uncertainty — which rows did you drop, and why?



None of these appear in a confidence interval. All of them typically dominate it.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Four intervals, routinely confused



Interval
Covers
Shrinks with \(n\)?




Confidence
A parameter, over repeated sampling
Yes


Credible
A parameter, given prior and data
Yes


Prediction
A future observation
No


Tolerance
A stated proportion of the population
No




The prediction interval does not shrink to zero because the irreducible noise does not go away. Forecasting audiences want this one and analysts hand them the first one.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Multiverse and specification curves

Enumerate every defensible analytical choice — inclusion criteria, transformations, covariate sets, outlier rules — and run all the combinations.


Plot the resulting estimates sorted by magnitude, with the choices shown underneath.


If the conclusion survives the multiverse, you have something. If it appears in eleven of four hundred specifications, you have a specification.


Week 8’s excess mortality project does this concretely: five to ten defensible baseline models produce materially different totals, and published figures almost never report the range. Comparing your range to a published point estimate is a bracing exercise.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Multiplicity, in disguise

Explicit. A GWAS tests a million hypotheses. Everyone corrects. Week 7.


Implicit. You tried a few feature sets, adjusted a window, dropped a bad year, and reported what worked. Same procedure — but the search was informal, so nobody counted it.


Collective. A field tries ten thousand strategies and publishes the survivors. Harvey, Liu and Zhu argue the effective threshold for a new asset-pricing factor should be a \(t\)-statistic near 3, not 2, because of the size of the collective search.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Sensitivity: quantifying “there might be confounding”
Every causal claim in this course must answer: how strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be to explain this away?


E-value — the minimum association strength, on the risk ratio scale, that an unmeasured confounder would need with both exposure and outcome. One number, easy to report, comparable against measured covariates.
Rosenbaum bounds — for matched designs.
Cinelli–Hazlett — omitted variable bias in regression, with contour plots.



This converts a vague worry into a quantity a reader can evaluate. Report it.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Calibration and proper scoring

A probability is calibrated if, among cases assigned 0.1, about ten percent occur.


Discrimination and calibration are independent. A model can rank perfectly and be systematically overconfident, or be well calibrated and useless for ranking.


Use a proper scoring rule — Brier, log score, CRPS — which is minimised by the true distribution and therefore cannot be gamed by shading your forecasts.


Week 13 pushes this furthest: sharpness subject to calibration is the objective, and you will find you have been getting it backwards.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Step 5 — references

Gneiting, T., and Raftery, A. E. (2007). Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. JASA 102(477). — foundational far beyond forecasting.
Gneiting, T., Balabdaoui, F., and Raftery, A. E. (2007). Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness. JRSS B 69(2).
Simonsohn, U., Simmons, J. P., and Nelson, L. D. (2020). Specification curve analysis. Nature Human Behaviour 4.
Steegen, S., Tuerlinckx, F., Gelman, A., and Vanpaemel, W. (2016). Increasing transparency through a multiverse analysis. Perspectives on Psychological Science 11(5).
Gelman, A., and Loken, E. (2014). The statistical crisis in science. American Scientist 102(6). — the garden of forking paths.
VanderWeele, T. J., and Ding, P. (2017). Sensitivity analysis in observational research: introducing the E-value. Annals of Internal Medicine 167(4).
Cinelli, C., and Hazlett, C. (2020). Making sense of sensitivity: extending omitted variable bias. JRSS B 82(1).
Harvey, C. R., Liu, Y., and Zhu, H. (2016). … and the cross-section of expected returns. Review of Financial Studies 29(1).

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
The question

How do you know the answer is good, using a test the answer could actually fail?


The emphasis is on could fail. Most reported evaluations are constructed so that they cannot.

title: Applied Data Analytics
section: The random split is usually the wrong split
text:
The random split is usually the wrong split

A random train-test split assumes exchangeable rows. Almost no real dataset has them.










Dependence
Correct split
Chapter




Temporal
Train on past, test on future
Healthcare, finance, energy


Spatial
Blocked by region
Geoscience, mobility


Group / cluster
Hold out whole patients, outlets, drives
Healthcare, NLP, reliability


Hierarchical
Hold out whole donors or sites
Genomics





The amount by which the wrong split flatters you is a measurable quantity. You will measure it at least three times this semester.


Three tiers: internal (resampling within development data — necessary, weakest), temporal (a later period, catching drift), external (a different site, cohort or instrument — almost always worse than expected, and that gap is the interesting number).

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Leakage: a taxonomy

1. Outcome-adjacent features. A variable recorded at or after the moment the outcome is determined.


2. Treatment as predictor. The operator already recognised the risk and acted. The model learns to predict the operator, and fails when protocol changes.


3. Preprocessing leak. Imputation, scaling, or feature selection fitted before the split. Small, silent, present in a large fraction of student projects.


4. Duplicate leak. The same entity in both splits under different identifiers — which is why Step 1’s entity resolution is an evaluation problem too.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Negative controls and falsification
The strongest evaluations are the ones designed to fail.


Negative control outcome — something your exposure could not plausibly affect. If you find an effect, your design is broken.
Negative control exposure — something that could not plausibly cause your outcome.
Placebo timing — run the analysis on a date where nothing happened.
Scrambling — destroy the structure you claim to detect and rerun. Any signal that survives is an artefact of the algorithm.



Cheap, powerful, and almost never done unless required. They are required here.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Measure your own instrument

Injection-recovery. Inject synthetic signals of known strength into real data, run your unmodified pipeline, and count recoveries as a function of signal strength.


The result is a completeness map: what your method would have found. Without it, “small effects are rare” and “small effects are hard to detect” are indistinguishable.


Astronomy does this routinely. Almost no other field does. Everyone should.


Week 6 is built entirely around this. Split the class: half compute an occurrence rate without the completeness correction, half with. Compare in the same session. It is the most efficient demonstration of selection bias available in any domain.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Evaluation must match the decision

AUC is a ranking statistic averaged over all thresholds, including ones nobody would use.


Decision curve analysis asks: at the threshold you would actually deploy, does using this model beat treating everyone and treating no one?


A model with AUC 0.82 can show zero net benefit at every plausible threshold. Students find this genuinely surprising and it permanently changes what they report.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Step 6 — references

Kaufman, S., Rosset, S., Perlich, C., and Stitelman, O. (2012). Leakage in data mining. ACM TKDD 6(4).
Kapoor, S., and Narayanan, A. (2023). Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science. Patterns 4(9).
Roberts, D. R., Bahn, V., Ciuti, S., et al. (2017). Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure. Ecography 40(8).
Lipsitch, M., Tchetgen Tchetgen, E., and Cohen, T. (2010). Negative controls: a tool for detecting confounding and bias. Epidemiology 21(3).
Foreman-Mackey, D., Hogg, D. W., and Morton, T. D. (2014). Exoplanet population inference and the abundance of Earth analogs. ApJ 795(1). — completeness correction done right.
Vickers, A. J., and Elkin, E. B. (2006). Decision curve analysis. Medical Decision Making 26(6).
Olofsson, P., Foody, G. M., Herold, M., et al. (2014). Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change. Remote Sensing of Environment 148.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
The question

Can someone else — including you in six months — obtain this number again? And who is going to act on it?


Everything that leaves your hands: the artefact and the claim.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
The one-command rule
$ make all

regenerates every number, table, and figure in the report from raw inputs.


Not “the notebook runs.” Not “here are the cells in order.”
One command, from a clean checkout, on a machine that is not yours.


Enforce from problem set one. Far cheaper to establish in week 5 than to retrofit in week 15, and the capstone rubric allocates 10 percent to it.

title: Applied Data Analytics
section: The parts you have not seen
text:
The parts you have not seen
You know Git and Docker, so this is brisk.


Data versioning — DVC, or content-addressed snapshots with checksums in the repository. A subset must be reproducible from the recipe, never shipped as a file of unknown provenance.
Explicit dependency graphs — Snakemake or a plain Makefile. The point is the graph, not the scheduler.
Environment pinning that actually pins — a lockfile, not a range.
Seeds — and the fact that stochastic algorithms are not reproducible across library versions even with a fixed seed.

title: Applied Data Analytics
section: Delivery: a claim, not a metric
text:
Delivery: a claim, not a metric


“The model achieved an AUC of 0.83.”




“Among patients admitted through the emergency department, this score identifies a high-risk decile with roughly four times the baseline readmission rate. At the threshold the ward would use, it flags about 60 patients per month, of whom around 18 are readmitted. It has not been validated outside this hospital.”



The second is the same model. It is also actionable, falsifiable, and honest about scope.


Nulls are results — report the interval, not the failure to reject. Ranges beat points — when the specification curve is wide, the range is the finding. And write for a reader who stops after the first paragraph, because they will.

title: Applied Data Analytics
section: The ethics of a ranked list
text:
The ethics of a ranked list
In week 11 you will produce a ranked list of entities suspected of procurement collusion.

At a base rate of one to five percent, and with your measured true and false positive rates, most of your top fifty is innocent.


You will compute and report that number before naming a single entity. The responsible output is a prioritised review queue with the base rate attached — not an accusation.


This generalises to every screening application you will ever build.

title: Applied Data Analytics
text:
Step 7 — references

Peng, R. D. (2011). Reproducible research in computational science. Science 334(6060).
Sandve, G. K., Nekrutenko, A., Taylor, J., and Hovig, E. (2013). Ten simple rules for reproducible computational research. PLOS Computational Biology 9(10).

title: Applied Data Analytics
section: Making large data fit: three techniques
text:
Making large data fit: three techniques

1. Columnar formats with pushdown. Convert to Parquet; read only the columns and row groups you need. A 200 GB CSV frequently becomes a 4 GB Parquet file you never fully read.


2. DuckDB over files. Query Parquet, CSV, and remote HTTP ranges directly in SQL, with out-of-core execution. You already know SQL, so this is free capability.


3. Principled subsetting. Bounding boxes, time windows, seeded stratified samples — with the recipe committed, not the file.

When you may use the cluster
There is a modest HPC allocation. Justify each request. Four legitimate reasons:


Irreducible scale — subsetting would change the scientific question.
Embarrassingly parallel simulation — the best use of a small cluster, and the recommended way to validate a method.
The one transformer fine-tune in week 10, which has a CPU fallback.
Once, for calibration — so you have felt the difference between eleven hours and eleven minutes.

Causal inference is the gate
Weeks 2–4 are an intensive block: potential outcomes, DAGs, confounding and colliders, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, sensitivity analysis.

Examined in week 4, separately and early. Twenty percent.


Format: four scenarios described in words. Draw the DAG, name the estimand, name the identification strategy, name the threat, specify one falsification test. No estimation required.


Students who can do this can learn any estimator later. Students who cannot will misuse every estimator they learn.

A leaked feature. A join that silently duplicates rows. A random split where a grouped split is required. An imputation that destroys the signal.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Data models



Origins of databases


Business data processing performed on mainframe computers in the 1960s and ’70s:

transaction processing (entering sales or banking transactions, airline reservations, stock-keeping in warehouses)
batch processing (customer invoicing, payroll, reporting).







History outline



1970-1980s: network and hierarchical models
1980-1990s: object databases
1970s-present: relational model
1990s-present: document model

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Hierarchical model



Information Management System (IBM)


Originally released in 1968, developed for stock keeping of the Apollo space program.
Represented all data as a tree of records nested within records.

works well for one-to-many relationships
not so well for many-to-many relationships
does not support joins

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text: Hierarchical model

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Network model



Conference on Data Systems Languages (CODASYL, 1969)



child record can have many parents
allows modeling of many-to-one and many-to-many relationships
uses access paths: sequences of links between records
queries are constructed by following access paths

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Network model



Bachman diagram

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Edgar Codd. A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks (1970)



A usable database management system should hide all the physical complexity from the user and expose instead a simple, clean model. This model should be based on tables, which gave birth to the relational model and the relational algebra.







Data independence


Data independence - the independence of application programs and terminal activities from growth in data types and changes in data representation.
Logical view on the data is cleanly separated, decoupled, from its physical storage.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Logical model


A relational database management system (RDBMS) exposes this logical model, together with logical building blocks for manipulating it, on top of a physical layer.
Thus, 2 layers:

Logical
Physical

In relational model, logical view is a table.





Note: query optimizer handles the construction of access paths (compare with manual effort required in the network model)

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Definitions


A relation \(R\) on a family of sets \((A_i)_{i=1,n}\) is a subset of their Cartesian product: \(R \subseteq A_1 \times \ldots \times A_n\).
A partial function between two sets \(A\) and \(B\) is a relation that associates to each element of \(A\) at most one element of \(B\): \[
\forall (x_A, x_B), (y_A, y_B) \ in p: x_A = y_A \Rightarrow x_B = y_B
\]
The set of all partial functions from \(A\) to \(B\) is denoted as \(A \mapsto B\).
The subset of \(A\) with the elements that do get associated to an element of \(B\) is denoted \(support(p)\): \[
support(p) = \left\{a \in A: \exists b \in B, p(a)=b\right\} = p^{-1}(B).
\]

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Set definitions



\(\mathbb{S}\) is a set of all strings.
\(\mathbb{V}\) is a set of all possible values. Contains anything that can be stored on persistent storage or in memory as a sequence of 0s and 1s and according to a convention to interpret these bits.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Set definitions



\(\mathbb{A} \subset \mathbb{V}\) – the set that contains all atomic values. Atomic values are values that are not structured, i.e., this excludes:

objects,
arrays,
lists,
sets,
trees,
bags,
etc.

but only includes:

strings,
integers,
Booleans,
dates

and so on.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Set definitions



The table itself, which can be seen as a collection of records. A synonym is a collection.
The attribute, which is a property that records can have.
The row, which is a record in a collection. A row associates properties with the values applicable for the record it represents. Synonyms of row are:

record,
entity,
document,
item.

The primary key, which is a particular attribute or set of attributes that uniquely identify a record in its table.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Table definition


Expressed formally, given a family of attributes \((A_i)_{1\leq i \leq n}\) and their associated domains \[
(Domain(A_i))_{1\leq i \leq n}
\] a table \(T\) is a relation over these domains, i.e. \[
T \subseteq Domain(A_1) \times Domain(A_2) \times \ldots \times Domain(A_n)
\]

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Table definition


A collection of records is a set of partial functions from \(\mathbb{S}\) to \(\mathbb{V}\). We denote the set of collections as \(\mathcal{C}\): \[
\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{S} \mapsto \mathbb{V})
\] Each record is thus modelled as a partial function mapping strings to values.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Table definition


A table is a collection with three constraints:

Relational integrity
Domain integrity
Atomic integrity

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Relational integrity


A collection T fulfils relational integrity if all its records have identical support: \[
\forall t, u \in T : support(u) = support(t)
\] Common support is a property of the table and contains the attributes of the table \(T\): \(Attributes_T\).
The extension of the table, sometimes denoted \(Extension_T\) is its actual content, which is \(T\) itself.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



No relational integrity

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



With relational integrity

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Domain integrity


A collection \(T\) fulfils domain integrity if the values associated with each attribute are restricted to a domain.
We define these domains with a function \(D\) mapping strings (the attributes) to domains (unused attributes are just associated with empty domains, i.e. this does not need to be a partial function): \[
D \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{V})^\mathbb{S}
\]
A collection \(T\) fulfils the domain integrity constraint specified by \(D\) if, for each row, the values are in the specified domains: \[
\forall t \in T, \forall a \in support(t): t.a \in D(a)
\]
Note: domain integrity still allows missing values.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Schema


Domain mapping \(D\) is called a schema.
Schema contains:

names of the columns
the domain or type of each column (string, integer, date, boolean, and so on).

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



No domain integrity

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



With domain integrity

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Atomic integrity


A collection \(T\) fulfils the atomic integrity constraint if the values used in it are only atomic values, i.e. \[
T \subseteq \mathbb{S} \mapsto \mathbb{A}
\]
This means that the collection does not contain any nested collections or sets or lists or anything that has a structure of its own: it is flat.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



No atomic integrity

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



With atomic integrity

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text: Relational model

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model

Relational algebra: a framework for manipulating relational tables

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Queries



Set queries act on relational tables as sets (as previously described): one can take the union or the intersection of two sets, or subtract a set from another. 
Filter queries take a portion of a table: some or all columns, some or all rows, etc. They are known as projection and selection. 
Renaming queries can rename columns.
Joining queries can take the Cartesian product of two tables, potentially filtering to match values from both sides. The latter is called a join.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Selection


A selection takes a subset of the records belonging to the table, taking a parameter, which is a predicate on the attributes.
The notation used is the \(\sigma\) letter. \[
S = \sigma_{B \leq 2}(R)
\]

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Projection


A projection keeps all records, but removes columns specified in the parameter list.
The notation used is the \(\pi\) letter: \[
S = \pi_{A,C}(R)
\]

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Grouping


A grouping, also called aggregation, merges records by grouping on some attributes, and aggregating on all others.
The notation used is the \(\gamma\) letter: \[
S = \gamma_{G,SUM(A) \rightarrow A}(R)
\] This groups by \(G\) and aggregate the values in column \(A\) (within the same group) with a sum
Note: there are grouping and non-grouping attributes.
Examples: COUNT, SUM, MAX, MIN, AVERAGE.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Relational grouping

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Renaming


Rename a column from \(A\) to \(D\): \[
S = \rho_{A \rightarrow D}(R)
\]

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Joins


A natural join is a filtered Cartesian product in which we only combine directly related tuples and omit all other non-matching pairs. The notation used is the \(\bowtie\) symbol: \[
T= R \bowtie S
\] joins \(R\) and \(S\) but only keeps records that coincide on the attributes common to both sides.
Joins are computationally more expensive than projections or selections.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Relational join

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Other joins



Theta joins explicitly specify the joining criterion instead of matching the common attributes, e.g. \(T= R \bowtie_{A=D} S\). Common attributes should be renamed, e.g. \(T= R \bowtie_{B=E \rho_{B \rightarrow E}} S\).
Outer joins keep records with no match on the other side, keeping the other attributes absent. Note that this breaks relational integrity in its strictest sense
Semi-outer joins are like (full) outer joins but only keep unmatched records on the left, or only on the right.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Normal forms



Atomic integrity
Each column in a record contains information on the entire record
No functional dependencies on anything else than the primary key

Normal forms help to address inconsistencies:

deletion anomalies: deleting a record makes the database inconsistent
insertion anomalies: inserting a new record makes the database inconsistent
update anomalies: updating a record makes the database inconsistent

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Key idea behind of normalization


Removal of duplication.






Downsides



Requires joins
Loss of locality (also called shredding)

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Limitations



lots of rows: beyond a million records, a system on one machine can start showing signs of weakness; even though more recent systems manage to push it a bit higher on a single machine (e.g., close to a billion)
lots of columns: beyond 255 columns, a system on one machine can start showing signs of weakness or even not support it at all
lots of nesting: many systems do not support nested data or, if they do, do so only in a limited fashion and it becomes quickly cumbersome

text:
Relational model



Alternatives





Issue
Solution




Lots of rows
Object storage


Lots of rows
Distributed File Systems


Lots of nesting
Syntax


Lots of rows/columns
Column storage


Lots of nesting
Data models


Lots of rows

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Drivers for change



A need for greater scalability than relational databases can easily achieve, including very large datasets or very high write throughput
A widespread preference for free and open source software over commercial database products
Specialized query operations that are not well supported by the relational model
Frustration with the restrictiveness of relational schemas, and a desire for a more dynamic and expressive data model

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Modern systems



key-value stores
wide column stores
document stores
graph databases

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Relational model



Challenges



integrity may not hold (nested/heterogeneous data)
ACID guarantees may not hold

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
CAP



Definition


CAP: presented as a conjecture by Eric Brewer at the 2000 Symposium on Principles of Distributed Computing and formalized and proven by Gilbert and Lynch in 2002.

Consistent: All replicas of the same data will be the same value across a distributed system.
Available: All live nodes in a distributed system can process operations and respond to queries.
Partition Tolerant: The system is designed to operate in the face of connectivity loss between replicas.







CAP (Brewer’s) theorem


You can have only two of the above.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Document model



Comparison



vs hierarchical: child data is stored together with a parent record
vs relational: use document references instead of foreign keys

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Document model



Pros



schema flexibility
data locality (performance implications!)







Cons



no joins
many-to-one and many-to-many relationships

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Document model



Schemas


Document DBs are not schemaless. They are schema-on-read.
Relational DBs are schema-on-write.

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Document model



Hybrids: JSON support in RDBMS



PostgreSQL 9.3 (2013)
MySQL 5.7 (2013)
IBM DB2 10.5 (2013)







Hybrids: joins support in document DBs



RethinkDB: relational-like joins
MongoDB: client-side joins

title: Databases: History, Models and Queries
text:
Graph model



Features

title: Big Data Analytics: Lab 10
text:
In order to improve performance (aka do profiling), one has to:

know where to improve. Here EXPLAIN helps
then apply relevant improvement methods. First and foremost, for analytic queries, this means indexing.







Important




Performance affects depth and breadth of data analysis.
Low performance may lead to subsampling.





First off, we start with EXPLAIN.
Fine quote:

“plan reading is an art that deserves significant attention.”

We can run several queries on lab10 DB:

explain select * from instances;
explain select * from instances limit 10;
explain select * from instances where "Bird" between 1 and 5 limit 10;

Example output:
 Seq Scan on places365  (cost=0.00..225.00 rows=10000 width=67)

First cost number is startup cost.
Second is total cost if all records are fetched. Units are cost units.
Width param is size of each row in bytes.

Bear in mind that the output of EXPLAIN is a tree with 2 node types: - scan nodes. WHERE conditions will appear as attributes to scan nodes. - additional nodes for joining, aggregation, sorting, etc.
Sometimes scans might have two levels: - The lower level will identify the row locations to fetch - And the upper level (bitmap) will sort the location prior to fetching



One can have more elaborate output with ANALYZE (adds execution time, among other things). Note that this will actually execute the query.
There is also EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) that shows cache and disk data sizes.




explain select i."Car" from instances i, metadata m where i.orig_id=m.orig_id and m.year=2023 limit 20;
Output:
                                   QUERY PLAN
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Limit  (cost=438.19..499.36 rows=20 width=4)
   ->  Hash Join  (cost=438.19..973.44 rows=175 width=4)
         Hash Cond: (i.orig_id = m.orig_id)
         ->  Seq Scan on instances i  (cost=0.00..496.00 rows=10000 width=14)
         ->  Hash  (cost=436.00..436.00 rows=175 width=10)
               ->  Seq Scan on metadata m  (cost=0.00..436.00 rows=175 width=10)
                     Filter: (year = '2023'::numeric)
(7 rows)
Hash join happens when rows of one table are entered into an in-memory hash table, in which rows of another table are looked up.




Different index types:

B-trees
hash indexes
generalized inverted indexes (GINs)
BRIN indexes
generalized search trees (GiSTs).

Indexes can be checked either via pgAdmin UI, or in psql via \d command.
More details: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-types.html


Useful when <   <=   =   >=   > operations are used. Also LIKE, BETWEEN, ~.
This one is used by default in Postgres, when no index type is explicitly specified.


create index bird_ind on instances("Bird") where "Bird" < 10;
create index bird_ind2 on instances using btree("Bird");
Now we can invoke EXPLAIN. Let’s first select all column values:
explain select "Bird" from instances where "Bird" < 10;
QUERY PLAN
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Index Only Scan using bird_ind on instances  (cost=0.29..270.27 rows=9999 width=3)
Find unique entries:
explain select distinct "Bird" from instances;
                                         QUERY PLAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Unique  (cost=0.29..295.29 rows=5 width=3)
   ->  Index Only Scan using bird_ind2 on instances  (cost=0.29..270.29 rows=10000 width=3)
(2 rows)



Now let’s apply index to a string column. First a query plan without index:
lab10=# explain select distinct source from instances;
QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------------------
HashAggregate  (cost=521.00..521.02 rows=2 width=10)
  Group Key: source
  ->  Seq Scan on instances  (cost=0.00..496.00 rows=10000 width=10)
Create index and check query plan:
lab10=# create index source_ind on instances using btree("source");
CREATE INDEX
lab10=# explain select distinct source from instances;
                                          QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Unique  (cost=0.29..219.28 rows=2 width=10)
   ->  Index Only Scan using source_ind on instances  (cost=0.29..194.28 rows=10000 width=10)
(2 rows)



What if we create another index on numeric column?
lab10=# explain select * from instances where "Car" > 1 and "Car" < 3;
                          QUERY PLAN
---------------------------------------------------------------
 Seq Scan on instances  (cost=0.00..546.00 rows=981 width=264)
   Filter: (("Car" > '1'::numeric) AND ("Car" < '3'::numeric))
(2 rows)
Create index:
lab10=# create index car_ind on instances("Car");
CREATE INDEX
lab10=# explain select * from instances where "Car" > 1 and "Car" < 3;
                               QUERY PLAN
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on instances  (cost=22.34..433.06 rows=981 width=264)
   Recheck Cond: (("Car" > '1'::numeric) AND ("Car" < '3'::numeric))
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on car_ind  (cost=0.00..22.09 rows=981 width=0)
         Index Cond: (("Car" > '1'::numeric) AND ("Car" < '3'::numeric))
(4 rows)
Note the Bitmap Heap Scan type.
Bitmaps are created ad-hoc for each query. Their contents depend on the query predicates.



lab10=# explain analyze select * from instances where "Car" > 1 and "Car" < 3;
                                                     QUERY PLAN                                            
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on instances  (cost=22.34..433.06 rows=981 width=264) (actual time=0.144..0.449 rows=981 loops=1)
   Recheck Cond: (("Car" > '1'::numeric) AND ("Car" < '3'::numeric))
   Heap Blocks: exact=362
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on car_ind  (cost=0.00..22.09 rows=981 width=0) (actual time=0.123..0.123 rows=981 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (("Car" > '1'::numeric) AND ("Car" < '3'::numeric))
 Planning Time: 0.112 ms
 Execution Time: 0.484 ms
(7 rows)
Buffers: shared hit=246 means 246 pages were read from cache, read means reading from disk.





Hash index uses equality operator only
However, doesn’t take much space
Uses a 32-bit hash code.

lab10=# explain select count(*) from instances where "Road" = 2;
  QUERY PLAN
-------------------------------------------------------------------
Aggregate  (cost=521.92..521.93 rows=1 width=8)
  ->  Seq Scan on instances  (cost=0.00..521.00 rows=368 width=0)
      Filter: ("Road" = '2'::numeric)
create index road_hash_ind on instances using hash("Road");

lab10=# explain select count(*) from instances where "Road" = 2;
                                     QUERY PLAN
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Aggregate  (cost=429.29..429.30 rows=1 width=8)
   ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on instances  (cost=18.85..428.37 rows=368 width=0)
         Recheck Cond: ("Road" = '2'::numeric)
         ->  Bitmap Index Scan on road_hash_ind  (cost=0.00..18.76 rows=368 width=0)
               Index Cond: ("Road" = '2'::numeric)
(5 rows)



Useful for composite types like text data, arrays or JSONB.
An example of an GIN index for full-text search:
create index on gadm using gin(to_tsvector('english',"COUNTRY"));
And query:
select count(*) from gadm where to_tsvector('english', "COUNTRY") @@ to_tsquery('english', 'United');
See more: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-textsearch.html.
These indexes need AUTOVACUUM from time to time.



BRIN stands for Block Range Index. BRIN is designed for handling very large tables in which certain columns have some natural correlation with their physical location within the table.
Usage considerations: - Good for tables with some natural order - Which contain huge amount of rows
Docs here: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-types.html




Query parallelization is controlled by various settings, some of these are listed below:

Parallel workers count/settings. Can be set by max_parallel_workers_per_gather like this:

SHOW max_parallel_workers_per_gather;
SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 4;
Some extra parameters can be inspected via:
SHOW max_worker_processes;
SHOW max_parallel_workers;
More info is here.

parallel_setup_cost: sets the planner’s estimate of the cost of launching parallel worker processes. The default is 1000.
parallel_tuple_cost: sets the planner’s estimate of the cost of transferring one tuple from a parallel worker process to another process. The default is 0.1.





Improve execution of queries from lab10 via indexing.

Try different index types.
Use EXPLAIN for decision making.

title: Distributed systems
text:
Distributed Systems Overview



Why?



Scalability: If data volume, read load, or write load grows bigger than a single machine can handle, it can be spread across multiple machines.
Fault tolerance/high availability: If application needs to continue working even if machine(s) go down, one can use multiple machines to give redundancy. When one fails, another one can take over.
Latency: With users around the world, it is desirable to have servers at various locations.

title: Distributed systems
text:
Data distribution strategies



Distribution


There are two common ways data is distributed across multiple nodes:

Replication: keeping a copy of the same data on several different nodes, potentially in different locations.
Partitioning: splitting a big database into smaller subsets called partitions so that different partitions can be assigned to different nodes (also known as sharding).

Both methods provide:

Redundancy
Performance

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Why?



Keep data geographically close to your users (and thus reduce latency)
Allow the system to continue working even if some of its parts have failed (and thus increase availability)
Scale out the number of machines that can serve read queries (and thus increase read throughput)










Assumption


Dataset is small enough so that it can fit on one machine.

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



S3 example


Types:

Live replication
On-demand replication
Cross-Region Replication
Same-Region Replication

S3 Replication Time Control (S3 RTC): replicates 99.99 percent of new objects stored in Amazon S3 within 15 minutes (backed by a service-level agreement).

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



How to handle changes?


Three algorithms:

single-leader
multi-leader
leaderless

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Single-leader replication flow



One of the replicas is designated the leader (also known as master or primary). When clients want to write to the database, they must send their requests to the leader, which first writes the new data to its local storage.
The other replicas are known as followers (read replicas, slaves, secondaries, or hot standbys). Whenever the leader writes new data to its local storage, it also sends the data change to all of its followers as part of a replication log or change stream.
When a client wants to read from the database, it can query either the leader or any of the followers. However, writes are only accepted on the leader.

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Leader replication

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Single-leader replication users



PostgreSQL (since version 9.0)
MySQL
Oracle Data Guard
SQL Server’s AlwaysOn Availability Groups
MongoDB
RethinkDB
Espresso
Kafka
RabbitMQ

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication

Leader-based replication with one synchronous and one asynchronous follower

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Synchronous vs asynchronous


Synchronous replication pros and cons:

Pros: follower is guaranteed to have an up-to-date copy of the data that is consistent with the leader.
Cons: if the synchronous follower doesn’t respond (for whatever reason), the write cannot be processed.

The leader must block all writes and wait until the synchronous replica is available.

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Semi-synchronous replication



It is impractical for all followers to be synchronous: any one node outage would cause the whole system to grind to a halt.
One of the followers is synchronous, and the others are asynchronous.
If the synchronous follower becomes unavailable or slow, one of the asynchronous followers is made synchronous.
This guarantees that you have an up-to-date copy of the data on at least two nodes: the leader and one synchronous follower.

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication

Google MySQL semi-sync

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Chain replication


Chain replication is a special primary backup system, in which the servers are linearly ordered to form a chain with the primary at the end.

The goal: “to achieve high throughput and availability without sacrificing strong consistency”.






Chain replication protocol



All read requests are sent to the tail (primary) of the chain
All write requests are sent to the head (a backup), which then passes the update along the chain.
Only the result of the write is passed down the chain.
Strong consistency naturally follows, because all requests are ordered by the primary at the tail of the chain.

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Chain replication protocol


The chain replication protocol considers only three failure cases, all of which are fail-stop failures:

Fail-stop of the head
Fail-stop of the tail (primary)
Fail-stop of a middle server

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication

Azure Storage architecture

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Problem: how to add a new follower?


Simple copy is not enough, because:

clients are constantly writing
hence, data is always in flux
locking the database would jeopardise high availability

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Adding a follower



Take a consistent snapshot of the leader’s DB at some point in time
Copy the snapshot to the new follower node.
The follower connects to the leader and requests all the data changes that have happened since the snapshot was taken. (Using a replication log position)
When the follower has processed the backlog of data changes since the snapshot, we say it has caught up.







Replication log position



PostgreSQL: log sequence number
MySQL: binlog coordinates

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Follower failure: catch-up recovery



Fetch the last transaction from local log
Connect to the leader and request all the missing data changes
Once changes are applied, continue functioning normally







Leader failure: failover



Determine that the leader has failed. E.g., use a timeout.
Choose a new leader. Use election process or controller node. This is a consensus problem.
Reconfigure the system to use the new leader.

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication

PostgreSQL example

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Failover: what can go wrong



asynchronous replication: new leader might be stale
discarding writes might cause problems in secondary storage systems
split brain: two nodes believe they are the leader
unnecessary failovers due to wrong timeout

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication logs



Statement-based


Log each write request (statement) and send it to followers.
Possible issues:

nondeterministic functions like RAND() or NOW()
broken order (autoincrement columns, WHERE clauses)
statements might have side effects

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Write-ahead log shipping


For log-structured storage: log already is the main place of storage.
For B-trees: use write-ahead log.
Possible issues:

too low-level
storage engine coupling

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Logical (row-based) log replication


A logical log for a relational database is usually a sequence of records describing writes to database tables at the granularity of a row:

For an inserted row, the log contains the new values of all columns.
For a deleted row, the log contains enough information to uniquely identify the row that was deleted.
For an updated row, the log contains enough information to uniquely identify the updated row, and the new values of all columns.

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Replication lag: consistency


Client-side consistency has to do with how and when observers see updates made to a data object in the storage systems.
Types:

Strong consistency: after the update completes, any subsequent access will return the updated value.
Weak consistency: the system does not guarantee that subsequent accesses will return the updated value; for this number of conditions need to be met. The required timeout is called inconsistency window.
Eventual consistency: the storage system guarantees that if no new updates are made to the object, eventually all accesses will return the last updated value.

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Replication lag: eventual consistency types


Types:

Causal: if process A has communicated to process B that it has updated a data item, the latter will always get updated values, and writes will supersede earlier ones
Read-your-writes: a process A, after it has updated a data item, will never see an older value.
Session: as long as the session exists, the system guarantees read-your-writes consistency.
Monotonic read: if a process has seen a particular value for the object, any subsequent accesses will never return any previous values.
Monotonic write: writes by the same process are serialized.

text:

text:

Replication

Advantages:

Performance
Tolerance of datacenter outages
Tolerance of network problems

Multi-leader write conflict

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Convergent conflict resolution



Give each write a unique ID, pick the write with the highest ID as the winner. Last write wins (LWW).
Give each replica a unique ID, and let writes that originated at a higher-numbered replica always take precedence over writes that originated at a lower- numbered replica.
Somehow merge the values together - for instance, order them alphabetically and then concatenate them.
Record the conflict in an explicit data structure that preserves all information, and write application code that resolves the conflict at some later time (perhaps by prompting the user).

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Quorum



If there are \(n\) replicas, every write must be confirmed by \(w\) nodes to be considered successful, and we must query at least \(r\) nodes for each read.
As long as \(w + r > n\), we expect to get an up-to-date value when reading, because at least one of the \(r\) nodes we’re reading from must be up to date.
Reads and writes that obey these \(r\) and \(w\) values are called quorum reads and writes.
One can think of \(r\) and \(w\) as the minimum number of votes required for the read or write to be valid.

title: Distributed systems
text:
Replication



Quorum: tolerating unavailable nodes


\(w + r > n\) is called a quorum condition.

If \(w < n\), we can still process writes if a node is unavailable.
If \(r < n\), we can still process reads if a node is unavailable.
With \(n = 3, w = 2, r = 2\) we can tolerate one unavailable node.
With \(n = 5, w = 3, r = 3\) we can tolerate two unavailable nodes.
Normally, reads and writes are always sent to all \(n\) replicas in parallel. The parameters \(w\) and \(r\) determine how many nodes we wait for.

A cluster is a group of connected servers that work together as a single system to provide high availability, scalability, and increased performance for applications. The nodes in a cluster are connected through a network and share resources to provide a unified, highly available solution.

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts



Architecture



a Kubernetes cluster consists of a set of servers (VMs/bare metal)
each server is either a master or a *worker.**
small and odd number of masters
no limit on worker nodes
worker nodes run pods
pods in turn run containers (one or more)
ReplicaSets are collection of identical pods

Pods

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts



Kubernetes architecture: the nodes



The nodes executing our containers run a collection of services:

a container Engine (typically Docker)
kubelet (the “node agent”)
kube-proxy (a necessary but not sufficient network component)

Nodes were formerly called “minions”
(You might see that word in older articles or documentation)

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts



Kubernetes architecture: the control plane



The Kubernetes logic (its “brains”) is a collection of services:

the API server (our point of entry to everything!)
core services like the scheduler and controller manager
etcd (a highly available key/value store; the “database” of Kubernetes)

Together, these services form the control plane of our cluster
The control plane is also called the “master”

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts



Running the control plane on special nodes



It is common to reserve a dedicated node for the control plane
(Except for single-node development clusters, like when using minikube)
This node is then called a “master”
(Yes, this is ambiguous: is the “master” a node, or the whole control plane?)
Normal applications are restricted from running on this node
(By using a mechanism called “taints”)
When high availability is required, each service of the control plane must be resilient
The control plane is then replicated on multiple nodes
(This is sometimes called a “multi-master” setup)

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts



Running the control plane outside containers



The services of the control plane can run in or out of containers
For instance: since etcd is a critical service, some people deploy it directly on a dedicated cluster (without containers)
(This is illustrated on the first “super complicated” schema)
In some hosted Kubernetes offerings (e.g. AKS, GKE, EKS), the control plane is invisible
(We only “see” a Kubernetes API endpoint)
In that case, there is no “master node”

For this reason, it is more accurate to say “control plane” rather than “master.”

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts



How many nodes should a cluster have?



There is no particular constraint
(no need to have an odd number of nodes for quorum)
A cluster can have zero nodes
(but then it won’t be able to start any pods)
For testing and development, having a single node is fine
For production, make sure that you have extra capacity
(so that your workload still fits if you lose a node or a group of nodes)
Kubernetes is tested with up to 5000 nodes
(however, running a cluster of that size requires a lot of tuning)

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts



Do we need to run Docker at all?


No!

The Docker Engine used to be the default option to run containers with Kubernetes
Support for Docker (specifically: dockershim) was removed in Kubernetes 1.24
We can leverage other pluggable runtimes through the Container Runtime Interface

We could also use rkt (“Rocket”) from CoreOS

(deprecated)

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts



Some runtimes available through CRI



containerd

maintained by Docker, IBM, and community
used by Docker Engine, microk8s, k3s, GKE; also standalone
comes with its own CLI, ctr

CRI-O:

maintained by Red Hat, SUSE, and community
used by OpenShift and Kubic
designed specifically as a minimal runtime for Kubernetes

And more

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts



Do we need to run Docker at all?


Yes!


We will need to build images and ship them around
We can do these things without Docker  (but with some languages/frameworks, it might be much harder)
Docker is still the most stable container engine today  (but other options are maturing very quickly)

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts



Do we need to run Docker at all?



On our Kubernetes clusters:
Not anymore
On our development environments, CI pipelines … :
Yes, almost certainly

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts



Interacting with Kubernetes



We will interact with our Kubernetes cluster through the Kubernetes API
The Kubernetes API is (mostly) RESTful
It allows us to create, read, update, delete resources
A few common resource types are:

node (a machine — physical or virtual — in our cluster)
pod (group of containers running together on a node)
service (stable network endpoint to connect to one or multiple containers)

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts

Node, pod, container

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts



Scaling



How would we scale the pod shown on the previous slide?
Do create additional pods

each pod can be on a different node
each pod will have its own IP address

Do not add more NGINX containers in the pod

all the NGINX containers would be on the same node
they would all have the same IP address (resulting in Address already in use errors)

title: Kubernetes part 1
text:
Kubernetes concepts



Together or separate



Should we put e.g. a web application server and a cache together?  (“cache” being something like e.g. Memcached or Redis)
Putting them in the same pod means:

they have to be scaled together
they can communicate very efficiently over localhost

Putting them in different pods means:

they can be scaled separately
they must communicate over remote IP addresses (incurring more latency, lower performance)

Both scenarios can make sense, depending on our goals
